events.text: The second tail came in the spring, and with it an itch behind the eyes that will not go away. Tonight you sit at the edge of a flooded paddy with the moon behind you and look at your own face in the water, and think of a human one, as hard as you can. The water wrinkles. Something looks back at you that has a nose like a person's and ears like yours, and far too many teeth.

choices.text: Copy the face of the old mourner who leaves rice cakes on your grave at Chuseok

effects.log: A tired, kind face with a mole by the mouth. You hold it for the space of three breaths and it slides off like wet paper. But it was a face. A kind one, to begin with.

choices.text: Make a face of nobody: plain, forgettable, the face of a crowd

ok.log: Nobody in particular looks back at you from the paddy. You could walk past yourself in a market. It is, the vixen who raised you would have said, the cleverest face there is.

fail.log: The face of nobody keeps turning into the face of the headman, who has a squint. You practise until dawn. The squint goes. Mostly.

choices.text: Give it up for tonight and hunt frogs. Faces can wait

effects.log: You eat four frogs and a vole and feel much better. But at dawn, curled in the earth, the itch behind your eyes is still there.

events.text: A face is not enough. A person on the road has clothes, a bundle, shoes, a way of walking that does not lift the heels. You have fur, which does not count, and a tail that keeps coming back like a bad habit. In the next valley a farmhouse has its washing out on the hedge: a hemp jacket, a pair of trousers, a headcloth, steaming in the sun.

choices.text: Take the washing. The family will think it was the wind

effects.log: You take it in your teeth and run. The jacket smells of a stranger's sweat and woodsmoke. That night the farmer's wife beats her son for losing it, and you hear it from the hill.

choices.text: Take the coat off the scarecrow in the barley instead

effects.log: A coat older than you, with straw coming out of the elbows. You will look like a beggar, which is the second cleverest face there is. The scarecrow stands naked in the barley all summer, and the crows are delighted.

choices.text: Weave the clothes out of the bead's light, the way the old foxes do

effects.log: It costs you light, and the cloth flickers at the hem if anyone looks too long. But it is yours, and it smells of nobody. You practise walking in it round the mound until the moon sets.

events.text: Market day, the fifth of the month: the five-day market at the river town, where three valleys come to sell. You walk in at noon on two legs, with a pheasant over your shoulder to trade and a face you have practised for a year. Rice-sellers, a knife-grinder, a man selling straw sandals off a pole, children everywhere, and {npc}, who sells rice from three open sacks, looking at your pheasant.

choices.text: Trade the pheasant for rice, and say as little as possible

mem.note: traded a fine pheasant for rice

ok.log: {npc} weighs the bird, argues for form's sake, and pours you a measure of rice without looking twice. Nobody looks twice. You walk out of the market with rice you cannot eat and your heart going like a hare's. It is the most frightening day of your life.

fail.log: {npc} looks twice. Once at the pheasant, once at your hands, which are counting on their fingers in a way hands do not. "You are not from round here," {npc} says. You agree, take the rice, and leave by the back of the market. But {npc} did take you for a person, at first. That counts.

choices.text: Do not trade at all. Walk the whole market twice, and watch how people do it

effects.log: How they haggle, how they bow less to the young and more to the old, how they never look at each other's eyes for long. A child bumps into you and says "sorry, uncle-or-auntie" without looking up. You were taken for a person. You go home and practise bowing.

choices.text: Give the pheasant to {npc} for nothing and walk away

mem.note: gave me a pheasant for nothing

effects.log: "For nothing?" {npc} calls after you. "Nobody gives for nothing!" You do not look back. That evening {npc} tells the whole river town about the strange kind stranger, and describes your face exactly, and is wrong about everything else.

events.text: The second market day, and the river town's dogs have found you. One of them, a lean brindled thing that belongs to the knife-grinder, has stopped in the middle of the road with its hackles up and its nose working, and is looking not at your face but at the place behind you where a tail would be. People are starting to turn round.

choices.text: Walk on at the same pace, as if dogs bark at everybody

ok.log: The dog barks. You walk. The knife-grinder throws a shoe at it and apologises to you, and you nod the way you have seen people nod, and the market forgets in the time it takes to sell a cabbage.

fail.log: The dog comes for your heels and you jump higher than a person jumps. The street goes quiet. You leave the town by the shortest way, which is over a wall, and you lose a sandal. (-5 health)

choices.text: Crouch, and look the dog in the eye, fox to dog

effects.log: The dog looks into your eyes and sees exactly what you are, and decides it has urgent business under a cart. An old woman selling chestnuts sees the dog go, and looks at you thoughtfully for the rest of the day.

choices.text: Buy a dried fish at the next stall and throw it the other way

effects.log: The oldest trick in any market. The dog goes after the fish, and you go after your business. You have learned something about dogs and something about markets, and they are the same thing.

events.text: On the mound that night the face comes off the way it always does now, like a mask with the string cut, and you sit in your own fur with the rice you cannot eat beside you. The moon is up. Down in the river town the lamps are going out one by one, and in every house there is somebody you could have been.

choices.text: Scatter the rice for the sparrows. A face is a tool, nothing more

effects.log: The sparrows will be very pleased in the morning. You bow to the moon instead, the way you were taught, and the bead takes a little of the light. Faces are for using.

choices.text: Keep the rice in the earth, like a person keeps a souvenir

effects.log: It goes mouldy by the winter, and you keep it anyway. You do not tell anyone why, which is easy, since there is nobody to tell.

choices.text: Go straight back down and practise in the dark streets till dawn

effects.log: Up and down the empty streets on two legs, bowing to doorposts. A night-soil carrier sees you bow to his cart and decides never to drink again.

events.text: Every evening at dusk a student comes up the hill road past your mound on the way back from the village school, reciting under their breath so as not to forget. {npc} is seventeen and too thin, with ink on the fingers and a county examination in two years that the whole family has sold a field for. Tonight {npc} stumbles on the same line three times, and sits down on your grave mound, and puts {his} face in {his} hands.
events.arc: The Student on the Hill Road

choices.text: Put on a face and walk down the road to meet {him}, a traveller going the same way

mem.note: walked with me on the hill road

effects.log: You fall into step beside {npc} and ask, mildly, what the line is. {npc} tells you. You know it: you learned it under a school floor long ago. You say the next line. {npc} stops dead and stares, and then laughs for the first time in a month.

choices.text: Stay a fox in the grass, and say the line aloud from the dark

effects.log: A voice from the silver grass says the next line of the Thousand Characters. {npc} goes white, then says it back, then runs all the way home with the line safely in {his} head. By the next week the whole school knows the grave mound is haunted by a ghost who knows the classics.

choices.text: Leave {him} to it. Students are not your business

effects.log: You go down to the paddies for frogs. Behind you, on your own grave mound, {npc} says the line wrong a fourth time and gets up and goes home in the dark.

events.text: Every dusk now, the same road, the same stranger walking beside {npc} at arm's length. {npc} talks about the examination, the field the family sold, the schoolmaster who sighs. Tonight {npc} says it straight out: "I am stupid. Everybody knows it." In your mouth the bead is warm, and you know an old game that the old foxes play on this road: the bead held out on a breath, passed across, passed back. A season of a fox's understanding. Or a season of the student's breath, which would make the bead very bright.
events.arc: The Student on the Hill Road

choices.text: Let the bead pass on your breath for the night, to lend {him} its understanding

ok.log: The bead goes across on a breath and comes back at dawn, dimmer, and {npc} walks into the schoolroom the next morning and recites the whole of the first book without a stumble. The schoolmaster puts down the pipe and stares. You lent it, and it came back. (Lent, and returned)

fail.log: The bead goes across on a breath, and in the night {npc} wakes, frightened by the strange warmth in {his} mouth, and swallows. In the morning the bead does not come back. Half your light is gone into a frightened student, and a tail folds flat against your back.

choices.text: Draw a thread of {his} breath instead. {He} will only be tired

effects.log: The bead passes and comes back warm with someone else's breath, and it glows like a coal in your mouth. In the morning {npc} is pale, and blames the lamp oil and the late nights. You walk {him} home again that evening, and are very kind. (+1 Breath debt)

choices.text: Just talk. Tell {him} how you learned the characters, without saying where

effects.log: Under a floor, you say, listening to children. One character a night, for years. {npc} thinks you mean you were poor. "Then I can do it too," {he} says, and goes home to learn one character a night. It is slower than a bead. It is {his}.

events.text: {npc} is pale. Not tired: pale, the way the moon is pale on a winter morning. {His} hands shake over the brush and the characters come out like reeds in a wind. {His} mother has bought ginseng the family cannot afford. And on the road tonight {npc} looks at you sideways, and asks, quite casually, why you never carry a lamp.
events.arc: The Student on the Hill Road

choices.text: Borrow once more. The bead is nearly bright enough for the next tail

effects.log: Once more, in the dark of {his} room, while the house sleeps. The bead burns. {npc} does not get up for breakfast. You tell yourself it is the last time, and you do not believe it. (+1 Breath debt)

choices.text: Stop. Walk with {him} and take nothing, and let the colour come back

effects.log: A month of evenings with nothing taken. The colour creeps back into {npc}'s face like spring into a field. {He} never asks again about the lamp. You think {he} decided not to.

choices.text: Say you are afraid of the dark, and laugh

ok.log: {npc} laughs too. "A grown person, afraid of the dark." The question goes away. It will come back, you know. Questions on this road always come back.

fail.log: {npc} does not laugh. {He} walks the rest of the way a little further from you than before, and looks at your shadow when the moon comes out.

events.text: The schoolmaster has noticed. Not the pallor, this time: the brilliance. {npc} recited the whole first book, and then the second, and now writes a hand the county clerk would envy, and the old schoolmaster has stopped sighing and started watching the hill road at dusk with a pipe that is never lit.
events.arc: The Student on the Hill Road

choices.text: Walk with {npc} by the lower road for a while, out of sight of the school

effects.log: The lower road is longer and muddier and goes past the tannery. {npc} complains all the way and never asks why. The schoolmaster watches an empty hill road for a month and goes back to sighing.

choices.text: Walk past the school at dusk, in plain sight, and bow to the schoolmaster

ok.log: You bow. The schoolmaster bows back, slowly, never taking those eyes off your face. "A good evening for walking," the schoolmaster says. "Mind the old graves." It is not a threat. You are not sure what it is.

fail.log: You bow. The schoolmaster does not bow back. The schoolmaster looks at your feet, which have left no prints in the mud.

events.text: {npc} is waiting for you at the foot of the hill road tonight, not walking, with a face you have not seen before. "The master told me a story today," {he} says. "Out loud, in front of everyone. About a student on a road past the old graves, and a stranger, and a bead. The old story says a kiss, the master said, but it is only a breath. And when the bead comes to you, swallow it, and look at the sky." {npc} looks at you. "Is it a true story?"
events.arc: The Student on the Hill Road

choices.text: "Yes."

mem.note: told me the truth on the road

effects.log: One word. {npc} breathes out, a long breath, as if {he} had been holding it since noon. "Then I will think about it," {he} says, which is the most frightening answer anyone has ever given you.

choices.text: "It is an old story for frightening students. Come, it is getting dark"

ok.log: {npc} comes. But {he} walks a step further from you than before, and {his} hand is in {his} sleeve the whole way, holding something. A twist of salt, you think. The master has been thorough.

fail.log: {npc} does not come. {He} stands at the foot of the road and watches you walk up it alone, and you feel {his} eyes on the place where your tails would be all the way to the top.

choices.text: Say nothing at all, and walk on up the hill alone

effects.log: You leave {npc} at the foot of the road with the story. Behind you, after a long time, you hear {his} footsteps start up the hill, slowly, keeping their distance, and stop at your mound, and go on.

events.text: The last evening on the hill road. You both know it. The examination is in a month, and {npc} is leaving for the county seat in the morning, and has stopped at your grave mound in the dusk to wait for you. There is a lamp in {his} hand, lit, for the first time. "One more time," {npc} says. "The game. I want to see it."
events.arc: The Student on the Hill Road

choices.text: Hold the bead out on your breath, and let {him} choose

ok.log: The bead hangs between you in the lamplight, small and pale. {npc} looks at it for a long time, then at you, then breathes it gently back. "Keep it," {he} says. "I would only look at the earth." {He} goes down the hill with the lamp, and passes the examination, and never tells anyone. (Lent, and given back)

fail.log: The bead hangs between you in the lamplight. {npc} swallows, the way the master said, and turns and runs, and falls on the stones of the road, and lies there looking up. Not at the sky: at the earth, the hill, the veins of it running under the graves. "Oh," {npc} says. Half your light has gone into a student lying in the road, and a tail folds.

choices.text: Take the bead back first, and say: "You know what I am."

mem.note: let me go on the hill road

effects.log: {npc} nods. Neither of you moves. Then you turn, and are gone into the grass, and leave on the road one red-brown hair, which {npc} picks up and keeps in a book for years.

choices.text: Do not come. Let {him} wait with the lamp until {he} gives up

effects.log: From the dark you watch {npc} wait, the lamp burning down. At moonset {he} says "goodbye, then" to the grave mound, quite loudly, and goes. In the morning there is a rice cake on the grass.

choices.text: Come with the dogs' scent on you, so {he} will never want the game again

effects.log: You roll in the hunting household's yard before you come. {npc} smells dog and fox together, sees your eyes in the lamplight, and backs away down the hill. Something on the hill laughs, and it is you, and you do not feel like laughing.

events.text: Long years on, a procession comes up the hill road: a palanquin, runners, a magistrate's red umbrella. It stops at your grave mound. The old official who gets out is {npc}, white-haired, and {he} stands at the mound a long time with {his} hat in {his} hands, and then sets down a cup of something and a single book with a ribbon marking a page.
events.arc: The Student on the Hill Road

choices.text: Watch from the silver grass, and let {him} go

effects.npcPass: old age, a magistrate of three counties
effects.log: {npc} speaks to the mound, softly, for a long time. You catch only the end: "...and I never played games with strangers again, and I always looked at the ground." The procession goes down the hill. Ten years later you hear the bell for {his} funeral, and go and sit on the hill above it.

choices.text: Put on the old face, unchanged, and walk out of the grass to {him}

effects.npcPass: old age, a magistrate of three counties, smiling
effects.log: The runners shout. {npc} raises a hand and they stop. {He} looks at your face, which has not aged an hour in all those years, and laughs like the student {he} was. "I knew it," {he} says. "I knew it all my life." You walk {him} down the hill to the palanquin, at arm's length, like before.

events.text: The children have gone home. The village schoolmaster, {npc}, is standing on the step of the schoolroom as you walk past in your borrowed face, and says, quite pleasantly, "Come in. The kettle is on." Inside: a low table, two cups, books stacked against the walls, and a dog's lead hanging empty on a nail. "I sent the dog to my brother's," {npc} says. "For the evening."

choices.text: Go in and sit, and drink the tea

mem.note: took tea with the fox

effects.log: The tea is barley, roasted dark. {npc} pours, and drinks, and talks about the weather and the price of paper and the boy who cannot learn the character for heaven. Not one word about foxes. When you leave, {npc} says: "Come again. I am too old to be frightened, and it is lonely."

choices.text: Go in, and say at once what you are, before {he} can

mem.note: told me the truth in my own schoolroom

effects.log: "I know," says {npc}, pouring. "I have known since you began walking my student home. Sit. Drink. You may as well be polite, since we both know."

choices.text: Thank {him}, and walk on, faster

effects.log: "Another evening, then," {npc} calls after you, not at all offended. The kettle sings behind you all the way up the hill road.

events.text: Another evening of tea. {npc} sets down the cup and asks, without any warning, the question nobody has ever asked you: "Why do you want it? The face. The road. The students. A fox has the whole mountain. What is it you want from us?"

choices.text: "To be one of you. Some day. The old foxes say it can be done"

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly, as if you had answered a question in the examination well, but not perfectly. "Then you had better learn what we are," {npc} says, "and not only what we look like." The next evening there is a book on the table, for you.

choices.text: "The bead grows brighter near people. That is all"

effects.log: "Honest," says {npc}, "and cold. Like the graves." {npc} pours you more tea anyway. "Come back when you have a better answer. I will wait, if I can."

choices.text: "I do not know."

effects.log: {npc} laughs, delighted. "Good. The best students never know why they came. They find out." You walk home with the question in your mouth instead of the bead, and it is heavier.

events.text: {npc} has set you a task: the Thousand Characters, copied with a brush, all of it, one sheet a night. A fox knows the sounds. A fox does not know how to hold a brush in a hand that keeps forgetting it is a hand. The schoolroom children, who have been told you are a cousin from the coast, watch your ink go everywhere.

choices.text: Copy it, sheet by sheet, all winter

ok.log: Heaven, earth, dark, yellow. By spring your hand writes like a person who learned late and hard, which is what you are. {npc} pins the last sheet on the wall beside the children's, without a word.

fail.log: The brush keeps turning in your fingers the way a paw turns. One night, very tired, you write the character for fox without meaning to, beautifully. {npc} burns the sheet in the brazier and says nothing.

choices.text: Teach the children instead, the way you learned: by ear, from under a floor

effects.log: You chant, they chant. A fox's ear makes a good teacher's. By the end of the winter the slowest boy knows the first hundred characters, and calls you "teacher" at the market, which nobody has ever called you.

events.text: The schoolroom is full of songpyeon and children: a book finished, the little feast the village school keeps when a pupil gets to the end of one. But the schoolmaster, {npc}, is not at the head of the room. {npc} is in the back room on a mat, very old now, and has asked for the cousin from the coast.

choices.text: Go in, in the face {he} knows, and sit by the mat

effects.npcPass: old age, in the back room of the village school, on the day of a feast
effects.log: "You came," {npc} says. "Good. The book on the shelf is yours. I wrote your name in it, the one you use. It is a good name. Keep it." The children's chanting comes through the wall. {npc} goes to sleep in the middle of it, and does not wake.

choices.text: Go in as you are, a fox with all your tails, so {he} can see you once

effects.npcPass: old age, in the back room of the village school, smiling
effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a long time: the red-brown fur, the amber eyes, the tails. "Oh," {npc} says, "you are beautiful. I always wondered." You lie by the mat until the songpyeon are all eaten and the children have gone, and the old hand on your fur goes still.

choices.text: Stay outside under the window, and listen

effects.npcPass: old age, in the back room of the village school
effects.log: Through the paper of the window you hear {npc} ask for you, once, and then tell the children to finish the songpyeon. You sit under the window until the lamp is put out, and leave a pine branch on the step.

events.text: Where the salt road crosses the county road there is a wine-house: four rooms, a yard, a mud wall, jars sunk to their necks in the earth, and a keeper, {npc}, who is eighty-one and has no one. You have been carrying {his} water for a month in a borrowed face, because {he} asked and you were passing. Tonight {npc} puts a ladle in your hand. "Somebody has to keep it," {he} says. "Travellers need somewhere to get to. It might as well be you."

choices.text: Take the ladle. Be the keeper of the wine-house at the crossroads

effects.npcPass: old age, in the back room of the wine-house, the spring after

mem.note: gave the crossroads house to the quiet one who carried my water

effects.log: You keep it. {npc} teaches you the jars all winter and dies in the spring, in the back room, holding your sleeve. The county comes to the funeral and drinks to {him} from {his} own jars, poured by a stranger they will know for the rest of their lives.

choices.text: Say no. A face that stays in one place gets looked at

effects.log: {npc} nods as if {he} expected it. In the spring the wine-house goes to a nephew who waters the drink. You pass it sometimes, and the lanterns are never lit.

events.text: The face you took is a keeper of a wine-house, and the wine-house is real: you saw to that. It stands where the salt road crosses the county road, four rooms and a yard, and the jars are yours now, and the debts, and the roof that leaks over the second room. Travellers come in at dusk wanting to be fed and not asked anything. You understand that very well.

choices.text: Mend the roof yourself, in the face, in daylight, like an honest keeper

effects.log: Up on the thatch in the sun, with the whole crossroads watching the new keeper work. A carter shouts advice. You take none of it. The roof stops leaking, and the crossroads decides you will do.

choices.text: Light every lantern on the first night and pour the first jar free

effects.log: The lanterns can be seen from three roads. By midnight every bench is full and a ferryman is singing. Somebody asks where the new keeper came from, and somebody else says, "Who cares, pour."

choices.text: Keep it dim and quiet. A wine-house for people who want to be left alone

effects.log: One lantern, low talk, no questions. The people who come are pedlars, widowers, soldiers going home. They like you because you never ask them anything, and they never ask you.

events.text: The old jars are nearly empty and you have to brew. Steamed rice cooled on a mat, nuruk crumbled in by hand, water from the well, all of it into a jar sunk to its neck in the cool earth, and then you wait, and listen to it talk to itself. A fox's nose is very good for this. A fox's nose is also very sure, three days in, that something has gone wrong.

choices.text: Trust the nose: tip it out and start again

ok.log: The second jar comes up milky and sour-sweet and alive. The old ferryman who drinks here drinks a bowl, puts it down, and says, very seriously, that nobody has made makgeolli like this since the year of the great flood. From a ferryman that is a poem.

fail.log: The second jar is worse. So is the third. The fourth is only bad. The regulars drink it out of loyalty and pull faces you are not supposed to see. By summer you have it.

choices.text: Add a breath of the bead's light to the jar, just a little

effects.log: The jar glows faintly for a moment in the dark of the yard. What comes up is the best makgeolli in three counties, and everyone who drinks it sleeps well and dreams of moonlight on old graves. People begin to say there is something odd about the crossroads house. They say it fondly.

choices.text: Buy the old recipe from the keeper of the next inn, in exchange for a secret

effects.log: The secret you trade is where the pheasants nest on the east slope. The recipe is: more nuruk, less patience. It works. The next inn's keeper eats very well that autumn.

events.text: {npc}, an old soldier with one ear and a wooden baduk board under the arm, has drunk at your crossroads every market day for a year, and played against everyone, and beaten everyone. Tonight {he} sets the board on the low table in front of you and puts down the black stones. "The keeper," {npc} says. "You never play. Play."

choices.text: Play properly. You have watched a hundred years of games through windows

mem.note: beat me at baduk

ok.log: You win by three stones. {npc} looks at the board for a long time, then at you. "Nobody plays like that," {he} says, "who learned it in one life." You laugh as if it were a joke. {He} comes back every market day after that, to lose.

mem.note: played baduk badly with me and laughed about it

fail.log: You lose by twenty stones. {npc} is delighted, and explains every one of your mistakes in great detail, with stories from three wars. It is the happiest you have ever seen {him}.

choices.text: Play badly on purpose, and let {him} teach you

mem.note: taught the keeper baduk

effects.log: A lesson a week for a year. {npc} is a terrible teacher and a wonderful storyteller, and every lesson becomes a story about a fort in the north and a friend who did not come back. You learn very little baduk.

events.text: {npc}, the widowed ferryman, comes up from the river every evening at the same hour, drinks two bowls, never three, and talks about {his} late spouse to whoever is behind the counter. Tonight it is the anniversary of the death, and {npc} does not talk. {He} sits with the third bowl in front of {him}, untouched, poured for someone who is not there.

choices.text: Sit down across from {him} and take the third bowl yourself, as the guest, and pour it out for the dead

mem.note: drank the third bowl with me

effects.log: You pour it out slowly on the earth floor. {npc} watches you do it and starts, after a while, to talk: how they met at the ferry, how they quarrelled about the price of rope. When the bowl is empty {npc} goes home, lighter. Every year after, on that night, there is a third bowl, and you pour it out for them.

choices.text: Leave {him} alone with it, and keep the lamp lit late

effects.log: You sweep round {him} and say nothing. At midnight {npc} pours the third bowl out on the earth of the yard, bows to it, and goes. You put out the lamp. It is not your grief. You are glad to have kept the lamp.

choices.text: Ask {him} what the lost one was like, and listen the way a fox listens

ok.log: You listen with every hair. {npc} talks till the cock crows. You learn more about being human from one ferryman's marriage than from a hundred years under floors.

fail.log: {npc} looks up in the middle of a sentence and says, "Your eyes catch the lamp, keeper. Like a cat's." Then {he} shakes {his} head and goes on talking, and you sit with your back to the lamp for the rest of the night.

events.text: A pedlar with a pack of needles and a big grey hunting dog comes in out of the rain and sits by the door. The dog does not sit. The dog stands in the middle of the floor with its legs braced and its lip up, looking at the keeper, and makes a sound in its chest like a cart on a wooden bridge. Every bowl in the room stops halfway to a mouth.

choices.text: Laugh, and say dogs never like the one who keeps the meat

ok.log: The room laughs, because it is true of most keepers. The pedlar drags the dog out by the scruff to the shed. The bowls go back to mouths. Your heart takes all night to go back where it belongs.

fail.log: Nobody laughs. The dog does not stop. The pedlar finishes the bowl quickly and leaves, looking back at you from the gate, and you know the story will be told at the next inn down the road.

choices.text: Put down a bowl of broth for the dog, slowly, and step back

effects.log: The dog looks at the broth. It looks at you. It lies down, still growling, and drinks the broth growling, and growls itself to sleep. The pedlar says it has never done that before. Neither have you.

choices.text: Go out to the jars in the yard and stay out there until they leave

effects.log: An hour in the rain among the jars, pretending to check them. The ferryman serves for you, badly, and charges everybody wrong. When you come back in, the dog and the pedlar are gone, and the room thinks you are very conscientious about your jars.

events.text: Twenty years and more at the crossroads. The ferryman's son poles the ferry now. A worn baduk board hangs on your wall, left by a soldier who stopped coming. Carters time their journeys to stop here, and a lost child from the hills was brought to your door last winter because "the keeper will know what to do". You did. The place has a name in three counties, and it is not your name. It is the crossroads house.

choices.text: Stay as long as the face holds. This is the best thing you have made

effects.log: You stay, and the place grows round you like a vine round a post. Some nights, closing up, you stand in the dark yard among the jars and feel almost like what you pretend to be.

choices.text: Start thinking about the next face: someone must keep it after you

effects.log: A keeper who never ages is a keeper who gets looked at. You begin to talk about a cousin in the south, a niece, a nephew, who will come one day. The crossroads nods. They will believe it. They want the house to go on.

choices.text: Notice how many of them you would miss, and be afraid of it

effects.log: The ferryman's son, the carters, the lost child who still comes back with chestnuts. A fox is not meant to miss anybody. You stand at the door at dawn with the broom, and miss them already.

events.text: A yellow dog has come to live at the house across the road from yours. It belongs to {npc}, a carter, and it is the ordinary yellow kind every village has, with a curled tail and an opinion about everything. Its opinion about you is that you should not exist. It has barked at your door every night for a month, from dusk until the cock crows, and the neighbours have started to ask each other why.

choices.text: Ask {npc}, politely, to tie the dog up at night

ok.log: {npc} ties the dog. The dog barks on the rope. But a tied dog barking is just a nuisance, and a nuisance is not a question. The neighbours complain to {npc} instead of wondering about you.

fail.log: "It never barks at anyone else," {npc} says, puzzled. "Only you. Funny, that." {He} does not tie it. The whole street hears {npc} say it, and finds it funny too.

choices.text: Make friends with it: a bone at the gate every night

effects.log: It eats the bones and barks anyway, with its mouth full. Dogs are honest that way: bribes do not buy a dog's nose. But it barks a little less at dusk.

choices.text: Hide the tails better. Hide the tails much better

effects.log: No lamps near your back. No sitting with your back to the moon. The dog still knows. Dogs always know. But the neighbours stop hearing anything in the barking except a stupid dog.

events.text: The yellow dog got loose in the night and got into your yard and got its teeth into the hem of your clothes as you came back from the hill at dawn, and held on, and would not let go, growling, while the carter {npc} came out with a lantern to see what the noise was. One kick would break its neck. One kick, in front of the lantern, and every eye on the street.

choices.text: Do not kick. Stand still and let {npc} pull it off

effects.log: {npc} drags it off by the collar, apologising. The dog is still looking at you over {his} arm as if it would give its life to tell everyone what it knows. Which it would. You go in and sit down and shake for an hour.

choices.text: Kick it. A fox cannot be held by a dog

mem.note: broke my dog's ribs

effects.log: It yelps and lets go. It lives, but walks crooked after. {npc} carries it home without a word, and the street, which liked you, likes you a little less, and wonders a little more.

choices.text: Turn over once, quick as a cough, so that it is holding only cloth

ok.log: For half a breath you are a fox inside your own clothes and then you are a person again, standing in your underclothes in the yard, and the dog is holding an empty coat. {npc} sees only a keeper who stepped out of a coat. It is a very strange morning for everyone.

fail.log: You turn over and come back a breath too slowly. {npc}'s lantern catches something red in the air for an instant. "Did you see that?" {npc} asks the dog. The dog, for once, says nothing.

events.text: The carter {npc} comes over with two bowls and a question, and sits on your step. "My grandmother," {npc} says, "used to say that a yellow dog sees what is under a face. That a great monk in the old days was afraid of yellow dogs, and that was how the court knew what the monk was." {npc} drinks. "Funny thing for a grandmother to say. Funny dog."

choices.text: "Your grandmother told good stories. Mine said foxes are afraid of salt."

ok.log: {npc} laughs and tells you three more grandmother stories, and you tell three back, and by the bottom of the bowl you are two people swapping nonsense on a step. Nobody suspects a person who tells fox stories.

fail.log: "Are they?" {npc} says, very interested. The next week there is a little dish of salt on {his} side of the road, by the gate, facing your door.

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth, quietly, on the step

mem.note: told me what the dog saw

effects.log: A long silence. Then {npc} finishes the bowl, sets it down, and says: "Well. You have been a good neighbour. The dog stays tied." {He} keeps it, as far as you ever know, until {he} dies.

choices.text: Say nothing and pour {him} another bowl

effects.log: You pour. {npc} drinks. Neither of you mentions the dog again, which is its own kind of answer, and both of you know it.

events.text: The yellow dog is old now: grey round the muzzle, the curled tail uncurled, too stiff to bark more than once a night. This winter it has taken to sleeping on your step instead of its own. You come out at dawn and it lifts its head, looks at you, and puts its head back down on its paws, as if to say it has told everyone for years and nobody listened, and it is tired.

choices.text: Let it sleep there. Put a sack down for it

effects.log: It dies on your step in the first snow, on the sack, with its nose toward your door. You bury it on the hill by your old earth, under a pine. You never thought you would bury a dog. You never thought you would want to.

choices.text: Carry it back across the road to its own house

effects.log: It goes on coming back. Every morning it is on your step, and every morning you carry it home, until the morning it is not there. The carter says it died in the night. You find you had been looking forward to carrying it.

events.text: A party of scholars on the way to the provincial examination stop at your table and call for paper and ink, and make poems on the spot, the way scholars do when they have had two bowls and want everyone to know it. The youngest, {npc}, writes four lines and reads them out: a poem about the one who served them, the one "with autumn in the eyes, who has seen more autumns than the hill". The others laugh and call it flattery. {npc} does not laugh, and is looking at you.
events.arc: The Poem That Gave You Away

choices.text: Laugh with the others, and ask for the poem to keep

effects.log: {npc} gives it to you without a word. The brushwork is very good. The last line has a character in it, half hidden in another, that only someone who reads closely would see: the character for fox. You fold it very small.

choices.text: Pour the next bowl and move away, into the shadow of the kitchen

effects.log: From the kitchen you watch {npc} watch the door you went through. The others are already on to a poem about the moon. {npc} folds the paper and puts it in {his} sleeve.

choices.text: Answer with a poem of your own, about scholars with sharp eyes

mem.note: answered my poem better than I wrote it

ok.log: Four lines back, quick as a cut, about a young hawk who sees a rabbit in every shadow and goes hungry. The table roars. {npc} flushes and bows. Nobody remembers the first poem now, only the second.

fail.log: Your four lines are good, and old: the grammar of a hundred years ago, which nobody uses now. {npc} hears it at once. "Where did you learn to write like my great-grandfather?" {he} asks, smiling.

events.text: {npc} came back, alone, on the way home from the examination. Failed, {he} says cheerfully: the examiner did not like a poem with a fox in it. {He} sits at the low table all evening, writes nothing, drinks very little, and asks you small questions in a voice that never changes: where you were born, what year, what your grandmother's name was, how old the jars in the yard are.
events.arc: The Poem That Gave You Away

choices.text: Answer every question with a careful, ordinary lie

ok.log: Born in the south, a year {npc} cannot check, a grandmother called Kim, like half the country. The jars are old because you bought them old. {npc} nods at every answer and seems, by the end, almost disappointed.

fail.log: One lie trips over another: the year you were born does not fit the jars you said you bought. {npc} does not point it out. {He} writes something on the corner of a sheet and puts it in {his} sleeve.

choices.text: Ask {him} plainly: "What do you think I am?"

effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a long moment. "Something old," {he} says, "that pours very well. I have not decided yet whether it matters." {He} pays, and leaves a better tip than {he} can afford.

events.text: Word on the road: the young scholar {npc} has been to the county magistrate, and the magistrate has a hunter with dogs in the yard of the county office. Then other word: no, {npc} went about a land matter of the family's, and the dogs belong to the magistrate's son. The road cannot decide. Tonight {npc} is at your table again, with a sheet of paper, and a brush, and a lamp {he} has moved to stand directly behind you.
events.arc: The Poem That Gave You Away

choices.text: Move the lamp back, gently, and sit down across from {him}

effects.log: "Thank you," says {npc}, and lets you. {He} writes a poem about a lamp that is moved, and a shadow that is not seen, and a guest who decided not to look. {He} gives it to you. You understand you have been forgiven for something, or warned. Possibly both.

choices.text: Let the lamp stand. Hold the face with everything you have

ok.log: The lamp burns behind you all evening. Your shadow on the wall is a person's shadow, exactly, and it costs you more light than a month of moons. {npc} looks at it until midnight, then blows the lamp out and laughs, at nobody in particular.

fail.log: For a heartbeat, at the edge of the shadow on the wall, there is something like a tail. {npc} sees it, and says nothing at all, and puts down the brush, and pays, and goes, and does not come back for a long time.

choices.text: Close the house early, for a sickness in the family

effects.log: You blow out the lamp yourself and send everyone home. {npc} goes last, and stands in the road outside a while, looking at the dark paper door.

events.text: Years later a pedlar brings you a book of collected poems, printed in the provincial capital, the work of a scholar who never passed the examination and became famous anyway. In the middle of it, between a poem about rain and a poem about a dead friend, there are four lines about a guest at a crossroads with autumn in the eyes, and a note in small characters: "I never found out. I am glad."
events.arc: The Poem That Gave You Away

choices.text: Keep the book on the shelf behind the counter, open at that page

effects.log: Travellers read it and look at you and laugh, because of course it cannot be you. It stays open at that page until the paper yellows. You never read it again. You never need to.

choices.text: Burn it in the stove. Some kindnesses are dangerous

effects.log: The paper curls and goes. You watch the fox character go last. It was a good poem. That is exactly why it had to go.

events.text: News comes up the valley the way news does, from a salt-cart to a well to a grave mound: the rich house at the head of the valley, which has three sons and prayed for years for a daughter, "even if she is a fox", has its daughter at last. A beautiful child, the valley says. Clever beyond her years. And at the wall of that house, on your night walk, you smell something you have not smelled since you were a kit in the earth: your sister. The bold red one, who always ate first.
events.arc: The House That Wished for a Daughter

choices.text: Go over the wall and find her

effects.log: She is in the women's quarters, a child of six with a red ribbon, sitting up awake in the dark as if she had been waiting for you. "Brother-or-sister," she says, in the old fox way that never needed to choose. "Do not tell. I am going to be real."

choices.text: Leave it. Her life is hers

effects.log: You go home the long way round. But you know the smell of that house now, and every time the wind comes down the valley you smell it again, and something under it, cold, like a cowshed in the morning.

choices.text: Watch the house from the hill for a season before doing anything

effects.log: A season of watching. The child is everything the valley says. The cattle are fine. The family is happy. You begin to think you were wrong, until the first frost.

events.text: The first frost, and the rich house's cattle begin to die. One a night, found lying in the straw in the morning, cold, with not a mark on them. The hired men say a ghost. The youngest son says the cattle die of looking at the moon. And you, on the hill, know exactly what is happening, because it is the oldest way there is, the one the stories name and this one will not, and your sister has always been in a hurry.
events.arc: The House That Wished for a Daughter

choices.text: Go to her, at night, and ask her to stop

ok.log: She listens, which she never did when you were kits. "Two more," she says, "and I would be real. But all right. A thousand days instead. Your way. The slow way." For a month no cattle die. You let yourself believe it.

fail.log: "You want it too," she says, bright-eyed. "Everyone in our earth wants it. I am just not afraid to take it." A cow dies the next night, and the next. She was always the boldest.

choices.text: Go to the cowshed yourself and guard it, every night of the winter

effects.log: A whole winter in the cold straw among the warm cattle, with your eyes on the door. She comes, and sees you, and stops in the doorway in her red ribbon, and goes away. Every night. No cow dies. You do not sleep. (-6 health)

choices.text: Do nothing. She is your sister, and they are only cattle

effects.log: The cattle die one by one, all winter. The rich house sells its fields to buy more. You tell yourself it is only cattle, and it is, for now.

events.text: The eldest son of the rich house, {npc}, sat up all one night in the cowshed with a lamp, and saw what came in, and told {his} parents. They did not believe {him}. They believed their daughter, who cried. Now {npc} is on the road out of the valley with a bundle and nothing else, driven out of {his} own house for telling the truth, and you are on the same road in a borrowed face.
events.arc: The House That Wished for a Daughter

choices.text: Walk with {him}, and tell {him} {he} was right

mem.note: believed me on the road

effects.log: {npc} stops in the road. "Who are you?" You say: someone who knows that house. {He} cries then, for the first time, and you walk {him} as far as the pass. "I will come back," {he} says. "When I know how."

choices.text: Give {him} food for the road and say nothing

effects.log: Rice cakes from a grave mound, wrapped in a leaf. {npc} thanks you without looking up. You watch {him} over the pass and know {he} will be back, because people who are driven out for telling the truth always come back.

choices.text: Follow {him} at a distance, a fox in the grass, to see where {he} goes

effects.log: Over the pass, three days' walk, to a temple on a mountain where an old monk takes one look at {npc} and says, "Ah. The cattle house." You go home before the monk can look at you.

events.text: Years later. {npc}, the eldest son, is coming back up the valley road, older, thinner, with a monk's blessing and four little bottles at {his} belt: white, blue, red, and one heavy as a stone. You know what they are. Every fox knows the story. You meet {him} at the foot of the valley. {He} does not know you. Up at the rich house the cowsheds stand quiet, and the parents have not been seen at the gate since spring.
events.arc: The House That Wished for a Daughter

choices.text: Tell {npc} everything: where your sister sleeps, which way your sister will run

effects.log: {npc} listens, and nods, and bows to you as to an elder. "Thank you," {he} says. "Whatever you are." {He} goes up the valley at dusk with the bottles. You do not go with {him}. You cannot.

choices.text: Go up first, fast, and warn your sister: run tonight

effects.log: You find your sister alone in a house of empty rooms, grown now, beautiful and very tired. "I know," your sister says. "I can smell the bottles from here." Your sister does not run. "Two more. And there is nobody left to take them from."

choices.text: Take your sister's place. Send your sister to the mountain, and wear your sister's face in that house yourself

effects.log: You put on your sister's face. It fits; you came out of the same earth. Your sister runs for the mountain in the dark, free. You sit in your sister's room in an empty house, with a red ribbon, and wait for the brother to come home with four bottles.

events.text: The brother {npc} comes home at dusk and stands in the yard of the empty house, and someone in {his} sister's face comes out to meet {him}, smiling, in a red ribbon, and it is you. {npc} looks at your face, the face of the sister who drove {him} out, and puts {his} hand on the bottles. Then {he} looks again, longer, as if something in the eyes is not what {he} remembered.
events.arc: The House That Wished for a Daughter

choices.text: Run. Through the white bottle's thorns, the blue bottle's water, the red bottle's fire

ok.log: The white bottle, thrown behind you: a thicket of thorns. You go through. The blue: a river. You swim. The red: a wall of fire across the valley, and you go through that too, burning, and come out on the mountain with your fur singed to the skin and your tails smoking. Alive. The brother stands at the fire and does not throw the last bottle. (-25 health)

fail.deathCause: fire from the red bottle, on the valley road
fail.log: Thorns, water, and then the fire, and the fire is too wide.

choices.text: Take off the face, and tell {npc} who you really are

mem.note: told me the truth in my father's yard

ok.log: A fox in a red ribbon, all its tails showing, in the yard. {npc} stares a long time, then puts the bottles away. "The stranger on the road," {he} says. "It was you." {He} does not forgive the house, or the sister. {He} lets you go. You run for the mountain with the ribbon still on.

fail.log: {npc} sees a fox, and that is all {he} can see. The white bottle: thorns. You go through them and over the wall and away, torn and bleeding. Behind you {he} is shouting the old story to the whole valley. (-15 health)

choices.text: Drop the red ribbon in the yard and go out by the back gate, now, before {he} decides

effects.log: You leave the ribbon on the stones like an answer and are over the back wall while {npc} is still looking at it. Nobody throws anything. In the morning the house is empty for good, and the brother sits in it alone, holding a red ribbon. (-6 health)

choices.text: Stand in the yard and let {him} throw. You took your sister's place. Take all of it

effects.log: You do not run. The red bottle breaks at your feet and the fire comes up round you, and burns, and burns, and you grow smaller in it, a fox, a kit, a cinder, a mosquito in the long summer light over a burned yard. Somewhere on the mountain your sister is alive, and does not know why.

events.text: From the hill you watch it happen, the way the old story always happens. The brother at the gate. Your sister running in her red ribbon down the valley road. A bottle thrown: thorns. Another: a river. Another: fire across the whole valley floor, and something small and red going into it, and not coming out the other side as anything you could see. In the long summer light afterward, there are a great many mosquitoes.
events.arc: The House That Wished for a Daughter

choices.text: Go down to the burned road at dawn and look for anything of her

effects.log: Ash, and a red ribbon, not burned at all, lying across the road as if somebody had set it down neatly. You take it to the earth under your mound. The mosquitoes follow you all the way and you do not swat a single one.

choices.text: Go down to the brother, and ask... no. There is nothing to ask

effects.log: You stand at the edge of the burned road in your borrowed face. The brother is sitting in the ash with the empty bottles, crying. You understand that nobody in that house got what they wished for. You walk away before the brother looks up.

choices.text: Turn away before the fire, and never look at the valley again

effects.log: You do not watch. You hear it, which is worse. For years afterward you go the long way round that valley, and you never kill a mosquito, and you do not ask yourself why.

events.text: A wedding procession passes below your hill: a bride in red on a palanquin, a groom on a white horse. The bride is the brother's granddaughter, and the procession goes the long way round the old house at the head of the valley, empty ever since, because the grandmothers say a fox lived there. Fox rain falls out of a clear sky as they pass, and the guests laugh and say it means a happy house.
events.arc: The House That Wished for a Daughter

choices.text: Follow the procession at a distance and keep the foxes of the hills away from it

effects.log: All the way to the groom's village, a red-brown shadow in the grass. No fox on any hill comes near. Nobody in the procession ever knows. That is the point.

choices.text: Sit on the hill and remember your sister, and let the rain fall on you

effects.log: She always ate first. She was never afraid. Wherever she is, a mosquito or a fox on some far mountain, and the brother's family is getting married in fox rain. You sit until the sun dries you.

events.text: Banya comes to the mound, the way she does once a year: the elder sister of the vixen who bore you, six tails, somebody's spouse in the next valley for longer than she cares to count, in a good quilted jacket and a borrowed face with a mole by the mouth. This year she looks at your tails, and at the dust of the river town on your paws, and sits down on the grave. "So," she says. "You have started. Then you had better hear the rules from me, and not from a salt peddler."

choices.text: Sit at her feet and listen

effects.log: "There is the old way," Banya says, "which I will not name, and you will not ask me to. It is quick. It is what some of your litter will try. Everyone who takes it is found out in the end, and it is never worth it." She looks at the village. "Then there are the slow ways. Come back next year."

choices.text: Ask her straight out how many of the old way she took, once

effects.log: Banya looks at you for a long, long time. "Enough," she says, "to know." She gets up, and brushes the grass off her good jacket, and does not come back for two years.

choices.text: Tell her you do not need rules. You are doing well on your own

effects.log: "So was I, at two tails," Banya says, and laughs at you, very fondly. "Everyone is doing well at two tails. Come and tell me that at five." She leaves a dried persimmon on the mound.

events.text: Banya, on the mound again, in the same jacket. "The thousand days," she says. "That is the first slow way. No one harmed, not a breath borrowed, not a hen taken from a yard that needed it, for a thousand days, and heaven counts. It counts more if you live among them while you do it. Avoiding people is easy. Anyone can be good on a mountain." She looks at the bead light at your lips. "You are not ready yet. You will be, at five tails."

choices.text: Ask her whether she ever kept it

effects.log: "Twice," Banya says. "Nine hundred and forty days, the first time. Six hundred the second." She does not say what happened on the nine hundred and forty-first. You can see in her face it was a child's warm breath across a room.

choices.text: Say you could keep it now, today

effects.log: "Could you?" She points down at the village with her chin: the hen-house, the sleeping farmer, the child with a cough. "Every one of those is a day. Go on." You look, and you are not as sure as you were.

choices.text: Ask what heaven gives a fox who keeps it

effects.log: "The ninth tail, clean," Banya says. "And after that, if you want it, the chance to stop being a fox." She says it lightly, and her six tails go very still behind her.

events.text: "The hundred days," Banya says. It is late in the year and she has come without the jacket, in an old one, as if this were a harder thing to say. "The second slow way, at the very end. You live in a house, with someone who loves the face you wear, and for a hundred nights they must never see you sleep. Not once. On the hundred-and-first morning you wake up with no tails." She laughs, not happily. "Everyone always looks. Nearly always on the last night."

choices.text: "Not everyone."

effects.log: "No," says Banya after a while. "Not everyone. That is why we keep trying." She takes your face in her paws, the old way, and touches her nose to yours. "Be careful who you let love you."

choices.text: Ask whether she is in her hundred days now, in the next valley

effects.log: Banya does not answer. She looks over at the next valley, where a lamp has just been lit in a farmhouse, and gets up, and goes, quickly, before it gets dark.

choices.text: Say that sounds like a cruel test, set by someone who never loved anyone

effects.log: "It is not a test of you," Banya says. "It is a test of them. Whether a human can trust what they cannot see." She thinks about it. "Nobody said heaven was kind. Only fair."

events.text: Banya does not come this year. A crow comes instead and sits on the mound, and then a fox you do not know, very old, grey, who says she has a message: Banya knew a fox once who got to ninety-nine. Ninety-nine days unseen. On the last night the one who loved that fox's face woke with a lamp, and looked. And the fox did not take revenge, the old grey one says. Went back to the mountain and left the house everything. "Banya said to tell you," she says. "She said you would know why."

choices.text: Go to the next valley and find out what happened to Banya

ok.log: A farmhouse with a lamp in the window and a person on the step, weeping, holding a good quilted jacket. You do not go in. On the hill above the farmhouse you find six-tailed tracks going up the mountain, unhurried. Ninety-nine, then. Her own.

fail.log: The next valley is full of farmhouses and none of them will say anything to a stranger about anybody. You come home not knowing, which is how foxes usually come home.

choices.text: Sit on the mound all night and think about the hundredth night

effects.log: The one who looked. The fox who did not take revenge. You find you understand both of them, which is new, and frightening, and might be the beginning of something.

events.text: {npc} is pale. You did that: one thread of breath, one night, and the bead is brighter for it and {npc} is not. {He} walks past the end of your street to the well every morning, slowly, stopping halfway to lean on a wall. Nobody thinks of you. Everybody blames the spring, which is very wet this year.

choices.text: Watch {him} every morning, and do nothing

effects.log: Every morning. The leaning gets longer. By midsummer {npc} is better: people mostly recover from one breath. You know that. You knew it when you took it. You watch anyway, which you tell yourself means something.

choices.text: Bring {him} medicine from the hills: wild ginseng dug by moonlight

effects.log: You leave it on {his} step in a twist of paper. {npc}'s family boils it and cries over it, because it is worth more than the house. {npc} is on {his} feet in a week. The village wonders who left it, and decides it was a mountain spirit, which is nearly right.

choices.text: Take another breath. One more, and the next tail

effects.log: One more thread in the dark. {npc} does not come to the well for a month. The bead is very bright, and you are very careful not to look at the well in the mornings. (+1 Breath debt)

events.text: An herb physician comes through the town and is called to {npc}'s mat. You stand at the back of the crowd in the yard in your borrowed face. The physician takes the pulse a long time, at both wrists, then looks up and round the yard, at every face. "It is a wasting," {npc}'s family is told. "The kind my old teacher called a fox's sickness. Keep a dog in the room at night." The physician's eyes stop on you, and go on.

choices.text: Leave the yard slowly, as if you had somewhere to be

ok.log: Nobody follows. But that night there is a dog tied in {npc}'s room, and the next night, and you understand that the door is closed now, and perhaps that is right.

fail.log: The physician says something to the family, and the family looks at you, and the whole yard turns its head the same way at the same time, like a field of barley in wind.

choices.text: Stay. Ask the physician, in front of everyone, what a fox's sickness is

ok.log: The physician explains, at length, with pleasure, to a whole yard: the breath, the bead, the old story. Nobody suspects the stranger who asked. You learn exactly how the pale ones die, and it is not a thing you can forget.

fail.log: "Why do you ask?" says the physician, pleasantly. You have no answer that is not a lie. You give one. The physician smiles at it.

choices.text: Go home and decide never to borrow from anyone who has a family watching

effects.log: It is a small rule, and a foolish one: everyone has a family watching, somewhere. You keep it for a long time anyway.

events.text: Someone from {npc}'s family comes to your door. Not angry. Holding a bowl of something, a gift, as people do when they come to ask a favour of a neighbour they do not know well. "They say," the visitor begins, and stops, and starts again. "They say you know the hills. Herbs. {npc} is so pale. I do not know who else to ask."

choices.text: Go back with them, and let the bead pass on your breath to {npc} for a night

ok.log: The bead goes across on a breath, into the one you took it from, and comes back at dawn dimmer. In the morning there is colour in {npc}'s face, and the family is crying into their sleeves. One breath given back. It is not enough. It is a start. (Breath debt -1)

fail.log: The bead goes across on a breath, and {npc}, half asleep, swallows. In the morning the colour is back in {his} face and something else in {his} eyes: a stillness, as if {he} could see the roots under the floor. The bead does not come back. A tail folds.

choices.text: Give them herbs from the hill, and keep the bead out of it

effects.log: Angelica root and jujubes, the honest kind. {npc} gets a little better. Not well. You did not give back what you took. You gave something else, and you both know it, though only one of you knows why.

choices.text: Say you know nothing about herbs, and shut the door

effects.log: The visitor goes away with the bowl. Through the paper of the door you hear the visitor stop in the road and say, to nobody, "They were so kind to everyone else."

events.text: One of the pale ones: {npc}. The same stillness at the well, the same hand on the wall. It does not get easier, the second time, to watch. It gets easier to not look, which is worse. Tonight {npc} is sitting alone on the step of {his} house in the dusk, too tired to go in.

choices.text: Sit beside {him} on the step and give it back, now, quietly

ok.log: On the step in the dark, in a borrowed face, the bead passes on a breath. {npc} thinks you are a kind neighbour with a strange remedy. In the morning {he} walks to the well without stopping. (Breath debt -1)

fail.log: On the step in the dark, the bead passes, and {npc} swallows it without meaning to, the way a tired person swallows. {He} sits up straight, looking at the ground as if it had just spoken. Half your light is in {npc} now. A tail folds.

choices.text: Walk past. You will come back when the bead is brighter

effects.log: You walk past. When you look back from the corner, {npc} has gone in. It is not the last time you will tell yourself you will come back.

events.text: You make a list, the way humans make lists: in your head, at night, on the mound. Every face you took a breath from. One sleeper after another, village after village. It is a short list. It is longer than you thought it was. Some of them are already old. Some of them are already in the ground, of other things.

choices.text: Promise the moon you will give every one of them back

effects.log: Every one, or their children, or their children's children. The moon does not answer. The bead in your mouth feels heavier, which might be the beginning of an answer.

choices.text: Tell yourself they all recovered. Most of them did

effects.log: Most of them did. You sleep well that night, the way you always sleep well when you have decided something comfortable.

choices.text: Learn their names properly, all of them, and say them over

effects.log: Names are a human thing. They stick in a fox's mouth like burrs. You say them over every night all winter until they come out smooth, and then you find you cannot stop.

events.text: In the next county there is another fox. You smell it on the wind in autumn, and then you meet it, on the boundary ridge at midnight: a lean grey-red fox with three tails and a bead so bright it lights its own whiskers. It has been living under the floor of a village school, it says, where forty students sleep in one long room before the examination. "One breath each," it says. "One a night. Nobody dies of one. I am at sixty-three."

choices.text: Ask what happens at a hundred

effects.log: "Heaven," says the grey fox, and grins. "A hundred breaths and the bead is a moon. Everybody knows the story." You know it too. You know the end of it. It does not seem to.

choices.text: Tell it to stop, or you will tell the schoolmaster

effects.log: It laughs at you. "You?" it says, and looks at the bead light at your own lips, which is not only moonlight. "Fox, I can smell the student on you from here." It goes back down the ridge, unhurried.

choices.text: Say nothing, and go home, and think about sixty-three

effects.log: Sixty-three. You count your own on the way home, and the number is smaller, and you are not sure whether you are relieved or jealous.

events.text: The grey fox comes to your mound. Eighty-one now. It is very bright, and very thin, and it has a proposition: the school has a new intake of forty, it cannot work fast enough alone, and the schoolmaster has started keeping a dog in his room at night. "Share the count," it says. "Half the students each. We both get to a hundred by spring."

choices.text: Refuse. And tell it the end of the story it says everybody knows

effects.log: "The hundredth wakes," you say. "Always. The hundredth one wakes and takes the bead." The grey fox looks at you for a long moment, and laughs, a little too loud. "Not mine," it says. "Mine will be asleep. I will choose very carefully." It goes.

choices.text: Agree. Half the count. Spring is a long way off

effects.log: All winter, two foxes under one school floor, taking turns. Twenty pale students go home at the new year and their mothers buy ginseng they cannot afford. Your bead is the brightest it has ever been. (+2 Breath debt)

choices.text: Agree, then go to the schoolmaster that night and warn the room

ok.log: An old schoolmaster, a stranger at the gate at midnight, a story about foxes. To your astonishment the old one believes it, wakes the whole room, and sets every dog in the village round the school. The grey fox goes hungry for a month and never forgives you.

fail.log: The schoolmaster sets the dogs on the stranger at the gate. You run. Behind you, under the school floor, the grey fox laughs and laughs.

events.text: Ninety-eight, the grey fox says, at your mound, at midnight. Its fur is coming out in patches and the bead lights up its whole face from inside, like a lantern made of a skull. "Two more. Come and watch. I want someone to see it, when I go up. I want a witness."

choices.text: Go and watch

effects.log: You lie on the roof ridge of the school and watch it go down through the gap in the eaves. Ninety-nine: a boy by the door, who does not stir. A week later, the hundredth. You watch it choose, very carefully. You watch it choose wrong.

choices.text: Refuse, and go and warn the room instead

ok.log: You get there first and knock the water jar over in the yard, loud enough to wake a valley. Forty students sit up in the dark. Under the floor the grey fox goes very still, and then away, and the count stays at ninety-eight for a long time.

fail.log: The grey fox is waiting for you in the yard. It is very much stronger than you now. You go home with a torn shoulder and the count is still ninety-eight. (-12 health)

events.text: The hundredth breath, in the next county, on a night with no moon. You hear it from your own hill, the way the whole valley hears it: one student sitting up in the dark and shouting, a lamp, dogs, and then a silence so complete that you know the bead has gone where the old story says it goes. In the morning there is a grey fox in the ditch by the school road, ordinary, one-tailed, very old, listening to the students recite.

choices.text: Go and sit with it in the ditch, for as long as it lasts

effects.log: It does not know you at first. Then it does. "The hundredth always wakes," it says, in a fox's ordinary voice. "You told me." You stay with it through the autumn. The students go past every morning reciting, and never look down.

choices.text: Go and look at the student who woke

effects.log: A plain, sturdy student with ink on the fingers, who now looks at the ground when walking as if reading it. They say that student will be the greatest geomancer in three provinces. You believe it. You walk past at arm's length and do not look back.

choices.text: Count your own breaths, there in the dark, and be afraid

effects.log: Your number is not ninety-nine. It is not small. You lie on your mound until dawn with the number in your mouth instead of the bead.

events.text: Long after, the grey fox's student, now old and famous and very rich, comes up your hill with a compass and a train of servants, looking for a grave site for a governor. The geomancer stops at your mound and stands on it, and looks at the ground, and then, slowly, looks at the fox sitting in the silver grass ten paces away.

choices.text: Sit still and let the geomancer look

effects.log: The geomancer looks for a long time. Then says, quietly, to nobody, "Not here. This one is taken," and leads the servants away to another hill. You are never sure whether the geomancer meant the grave, or you.

choices.text: Go, before those eyes that read the earth can read you

effects.log: You are gone into the grass. Behind you the geomancer laughs, an old, kind laugh. "Wise," the geomancer says to the hill. "Very wise. My old friend was not."

events.text: A geomancer has come to your hill with a compass the size of a dinner tray and a voice like a temple bell, and has found, on the slope just above your earth, the most auspicious grave site in the county: a dragon's vein of qi, a hill like an armchair, water on the left. The geomancer has sold it to the Pak family for their grandfather. You know this because yesterday, at the same spot, with the same speech, the geomancer sold it to the Choe family for theirs. And you know something else: the qi does not run there at all. It runs under your mound.

choices.text: Put on a face and tell both families, separately, that the geomancer is a cheat

ok.log: The Paks believe you and the Choes do not, which is worse than nobody believing you. The geomancer leaves the county by night with both fees. The two families now each own, as far as they are concerned, the same hill.

fail.log: "And who are you?" asks the eldest Choe, very coldly. A stranger with no family, no hill and no name worth asking. You leave. The geomancer smiles at you from the gate.

choices.text: Lead the geomancer astray with foxfire on the way home, into the deep paddy

effects.log: A light ahead on the dyke, always just ahead. By dawn the geomancer is up to the waist in the deepest paddy in the valley, holding the compass over the head and praying. The story goes round three counties. The fees do not come back.

choices.text: Show the geomancer, in a face, where the qi really runs, for a share of nothing

effects.log: You walk the hill together. You show where the cold breath comes up out of the old mounds, where the vein bends, where it pools under your own earth, and where it does not. The geomancer goes very quiet, and then asks, in a different voice, who taught you. You say: the dead.

choices.text: Stay out of it. It is a human quarrel on top of your roof

effects.log: You stay in your earth and listen to two families pace out the same slope over your head, one after the other, all autumn.

events.text: In the dark of the new moon, the Choe family come up the hill with a coffin and no torches and bury their grandfather on the disputed slope, fast and quiet, the old trick of a secret burial on a hill that is not yet yours. In the morning the Paks find the fresh earth. By noon there are thirty people on your hill with spades, shouting, and the Paks have started to dig the Choe grandfather up again, right above your earth.

choices.text: Bring the slope down a little under the diggers' feet. Not much. Enough to frighten

effects.log: The earth sighs and shifts. Thirty people stand very still. An old woman of the Pak family says, loudly, that the hill does not want either of them, and both families go home, and send for the magistrate instead of spades.

choices.text: Go among them in a face, as an old woman of the next village, and remind them of the dead

ok.log: You say: whoever wins this hill, the grandfather in the earth loses his sleep. A Pak puts a spade down. Then a Choe. They glare at each other across the grave and go home to write petitions instead, which is slower and kills nobody.

fail.log: Nobody listens to an old woman from the next village. Somebody pushes you into the open grave. You climb out with earth in your face and go home with a bruised hip and the shouting behind you. (-6 health)

choices.text: Move your earth to the far side of the hill until they have finished

effects.log: A week of digging a new earth by night, in stony ground, while above the old one two families dig and fill and dig the same grave. You do not miss the noise.

events.text: The county magistrate, {npc}, has had forty petitions about one hill and come up it alone, at night, with a lamp, to look at it without either family watching. You are sitting on your mound in a face, an old local who couldn't sleep. {npc} sits down beside you without asking, sets the lamp on the grass, and says, "Well. You live here. Whose hill is it?"

choices.text: "The dead's. Leave both grandfathers where they lie, and plant a pine between them"

mem.note: gave me my judgement on the grave hill

effects.log: {npc} laughs, and then does not. In the morning the judgement is read: both graves stay, a pine between them, and any family that moves a spadeful of earth on that hill pays for a well in the village. The pine is still there.

choices.text: Tell {him} where the qi really runs: under neither

effects.log: {npc} listens with the lamp between you. "And how would an old local know where qi runs?" The lamp throws your shadow on the grass, and you move, quickly, so it falls on a stone.

choices.text: Say you are only an old local who couldn't sleep, and leave the judgement to the judge

effects.log: {npc} nods and sits on your mound until the lamp goes out, thinking. You go home. The judgement is fair, for a judgement. Neither family is happy, which, a clerk tells you later, is how you know.

events.text: Generations on, the Pak and Choe families intermarry. At the wedding feast, in the yard below your hill, the oldest guest tells the story of the grave quarrel as a joke, and everyone laughs, and the two grandfathers sleep side by side on the slope above your earth, and nobody has dug anything for generations.

choices.text: Sit on the slope during the feast, and listen to them tell it wrong

effects.log: In their version a mountain spirit made the earth shake. In their version the magistrate had a dream. Nobody in their version is a fox. You like their version better.

choices.text: Go down in a face and drink to both grandfathers

effects.log: Nobody asks who you are at a wedding. You drink to the Pak grandfather and the Choe grandfather, and a child asks you which family you belong to, and you say, "the hill", and the child accepts it.

events.text: A monk, {npc}, with a begging bowl and a straw hat as wide as a cart wheel sits down on your grave mound to rest, takes out a wooden fish, and begins to chant: the short sutra, the one about emptiness. You are sitting a little way off in your borrowed face, being a traveller who has also stopped to rest. With every knock of the wooden fish, your face slips a little. The ears first. Then something at the edge of your eyes.

choices.text: Hold the face. Sit still, and listen to the chant all the way through

ok.log: Form is emptiness, emptiness is form. You hold on to a face that is neither, and somewhere in the middle of the sutra you stop holding, and it holds itself. When the monk stops, your ears are where a person's ears are. You have never felt so tired, or so clear.

fail.log: Halfway through, your ears come up through your hair like two bamboo shoots. The monk goes on chanting, steadily, to the end, and does not look at you once. Then puts the wooden fish away.

choices.text: Get up and walk away before the face goes

effects.log: You walk away at a traveller's pace with your ears in your hands. Behind you the wooden fish stops. Starts again. Stops. As if the monk is waiting to see if you will come back.

choices.text: Let the face go, and sit there as the fox you are, tails and all, and listen

effects.log: You let it go. A fox sits in the grass with its tails round its feet and listens to the sutra. The monk chants to the end without a pause, and then bows to you, deeply, as to another monk.

events.text: The monk, {npc}, puts the wooden fish away and turns the straw hat toward you. "What is your name," {npc} asks, "in this life?" Not who are you. Not what are you. Just the name. As if lives were a thing you might have several of, like coats.

choices.text: Give the name of the face you wear

effects.log: You give it. {npc} repeats it twice, carefully, the way one repeats a name one means to pray for. "Good," {npc} says. "I will remember it. It is a nice name. Try to deserve it." And picks up the bowl, and goes on down the road.

choices.text: "I do not have one. I am a fox."

effects.log: "Then you have one," says {npc}, delighted, "and it is Fox. That will do to begin with. Everyone begins with something." The monk laughs all the way down the hill. You sit on the mound and say your name to yourself, and it sounds new.

choices.text: Ask {him} the same question back

effects.log: "In this life?" {npc} considers it. "I have forgotten. That was the point of becoming a monk." The straw hat bobs as {he} laughs. "Ask me in the next one. I may remember better."

events.text: Every few years the monk {npc} comes back along the hill road, older each time, and sits on your mound, and chants, and you sit in the grass and listen. You have learned the sutra by heart without trying. This time {npc} does not chant. {He} just sits, and after a while says: "Sit with me. Not listening. Sitting. It is harder than it looks."

choices.text: Sit. Do nothing at all, beside {him}, until the moon comes up

ok.log: For a long time your mind runs like a fox in a field. Then, without your noticing when, it lies down. The moon comes up. The bead in your mouth is brighter than a month of bowing has ever made it, and you did not ask it to be.

fail.log: You last until a vole moves in the grass. {npc} laughs softly. "Good," {he} says. "That was very long, for a first time. I lasted until a sparrow."

choices.text: Ask {him} to teach you to chant, instead

effects.log: {npc} teaches you the wooden fish: the rhythm, the breath. You have a fox's ear. By dusk you can keep time with a temple. "Now you will never be quiet again," {npc} says, rueful.

events.text: The monk does not come back along the hill road. A novice does instead, a boy with a shaved head and a bundle, who climbs to your grave mound and looks round it carefully, and sets down on it a wooden fish worn smooth as a river stone, and says, to the grass in general: "The teacher said a friend lived here.
