The teacher said the friend has a name now. The teacher said, please keep the time."

choices.text: Take the wooden fish to your earth, and keep the time, every evening

effects.log: Every evening, at dusk, a faint knocking from under a grave mound on the hill road. The village says it is a ghost of a monk. Students hurry past. Nobody ever finds out that it is a fox keeping a promise for someone who is dead.

choices.text: Come out of the grass, in a face, and thank the novice properly

effects.log: You bow. The novice bows back, and looks at your face, and then at your feet, and smiles. "The teacher said you would bow very well," the novice says. "The teacher said you practised."

events.text: The mountain temple's jars of offering wine keep emptying, and the monks blame the young guest who boards there to study: {npc} of the Jeon clan, nineteen, much too clever, with a habit of laughing at sermons. The guest swears innocence. The monks do not believe a word. You know {npc} is innocent, because it is you: every dusk you carry a little of it off to the fox shrine in the woods, where the offerings were promised first. The shrine has never been so well kept.

choices.text: Stop taking it. The young one is being punished for you

effects.log: You stop. The jars stay full. The monks decide the young guest has reformed, and make {him} carry water for a month as penance anyway. {npc} carries it, very thoughtfully, looking at the jars.

choices.text: Keep taking it. The shrine deserves the best wine on the mountain

effects.log: Every dusk, a little. The monks put {npc} on rice and water. {npc} does not complain. {npc} watches the storeroom door instead, with an expression you will later learn to recognise.

choices.text: Go to the temple in a face and confess it was a fox

effects.log: The monks laugh at the pilgrim who blames a fox. {npc} does not laugh. {npc} looks at your face very carefully, the way one looks at a riddle, and says, "Thank you, pilgrim," with great politeness.

events.text: Dusk in the storeroom. You slip in under the door the way you always do, and the jar has been moved, and there is a rope on the floor, and before you can turn, the rope is round you and a square of yellow paper is pressed against your back, and every hair you have goes stiff. {npc} sits back on {his} heels, grinning. "An old man on the road gave me the rope," {he} says. "And the paper. The old man said a fox in a wine jar is a fox with a bead."

choices.text: Fight the rope with everything you have

ok.log: The paper burns your back and you tear free of it anyway, and the rope with it, and you are out under the door with {npc} laughing behind you. "Next time!" {he} calls. You believe {him}. (-8 health)

fail.log: The rope only tightens. The talisman burns like nettles. You lie still at last, panting, and {npc} pats your head, very gently, as one pats a dog. (-12 health)

choices.text: Lie still and talk. The young one is clearly a talker

effects.log: "You speak!" says {npc}, delighted. "Of course you speak. Tell me everything." You tell {him} some things. {npc} listens to every one as if memorising it, which {he} is.

choices.text: Turn over three times in the rope, and leave it holding nothing

ok.log: You turn, and the rope closes on a heap of straw. {npc} stares at the straw, and then laughs until {he} has to sit down. "Teach me that," {he} says to the empty room. "Please."

fail.log: The talisman holds your shape exactly where it is. You turn over once and land on your nose. {npc} is very kind about it. (-8 health)

events.text: {npc} has you, or nearly: the rope, the paper, the storeroom, the monks asleep. "The old stories say," {he} begins, very reasonably, "that a fox's bead, swallowed, gives a person thirty-six shapes. I would like thirty-six shapes. I have such plans. The magistrate of this county, for instance, has never once been turned into a goat."

choices.text: Give it. Let the bead pass on a breath, and let the clever one swallow

effects.log: You give it. {npc} swallows, and sits very still, and then turns into a crane, a pine branch, an old woman and a fox, one after another, and back, and laughs and laughs. Your bead is in a trickster now, and a tail folds against your back. You are not as sorry as you should be. (Bead lost: win it back)

choices.text: Offer a lesson instead: how to turn over three times. The bead stays

ok.log: All night in the storeroom. By dawn {npc} can turn over once and come up as a slightly different version of the same face, which is more than any human has ever done. {He} unties you with tears of joy, and you are friends, which neither of you planned.

fail.log: The lesson goes badly. {npc} turns over three times and lands in a wine jar. But {he} is laughing so hard {he} unties you to help pull {him} out, and you go out under the door while {he} is still dripping.

choices.text: Trick {him}: say the bead is hidden in the wine jar, and run while {he} looks

ok.log: {npc} has {his} whole arm in the jar before {he} realises, and by then you are out under the door with the rope trailing. Behind you, a long, admiring curse. A trickster knows when a trick has been played well.

fail.log: "Nice try," says {npc}, without looking at the jar. "The old man said you would say that." But {he} lets you go at dawn anyway, with the talisman, which {he} says {he} will keep for next time. (-6 health)

events.text: Years later the whole province tells stories about {npc} of the Jeon clan: a greedy magistrate's rice turned to frogs in the granary, a cruel landlord's ledger that rewrote itself in favour of the tenants, a king's banquet where every dish was a painting. Tonight {npc} sits on your mound in the moonlight, middle-aged, delighted with the world, and asks for help with the next one: a governor's treasury, and a hungry county.

choices.text: Help. Foxfire on the treasury road, and a governor who follows it all night

effects.log: The governor follows the lights into a bamboo grove and loses three cartloads of grain, which {npc} has already given away. The county eats all winter. A song is made about it, and the fox in it is very handsome.

choices.text: Say no. Tricksters end badly, in the stories

effects.log: "So do foxes," says {npc}, and laughs, and goes off to do it alone. It works, mostly. It works until the year it does not.

choices.text: Ask {him} what it is like, to have many shapes and one life

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it seriously, for once. "Lonely," {he} says. "Every shape is a lie, and the people I help only ever meet the lie." {He} looks at you. "But you knew that."

events.text: {npc} of the Jeon clan is grey now, and has been to the mountains and back, and has come to your mound one last time, without a trick in {his} sleeve. "I have been everything," {npc} says. "A crane, a cloud, a king's cook. It was the best life anyone has ever had. It is yours. Here." And {he} breathes out, and the bead comes back to you on the breath, warm, brighter than it went.

choices.text: Take it, and thank {him}

effects.log: The folded tail opens like a fan. {npc} laughs at your face and walks off down the hill road, one shape, an old person in a blue robe, and you never see {him} again, and in the stories {he} goes into a mountain and becomes an immortal. You think {he} would like that.

choices.text: Tell {him} to keep it till the end, and come for it after

effects.log: {npc} keeps it one more year, a crane over the mountains, and dies in a mountain hut in the spring. You find the bead on the doorstep, waiting for you, beside a note that says only: "Thirty-six. Thank you." The tail opens.

events.text: {npc}, the matchmaker who knows every family in the county, has come to your gate with a smile like a sunrise and a folded red paper. A proposal: the miller's eldest, a good worker, a good family, a good age. All {npc} needs from you is your four pillars: the year, month, day and hour of your birth, written down, so the almanac can say whether the two of you are in harmony. A fox does not have an hour of birth a human could write.

choices.text: Invent one. A good one

ok.log: You write down a year, a month, a day and an hour, all ordinary. {npc} reads the almanac and frowns, and reads it again, and says it is the strangest chart, a nine-fold fire in the hour, but harmonious. {npc} will take it to the miller. You did not mean it to be harmonious.

fail.log: You write down an hour that does not exist. {npc} looks at it, then at you, then laughs and says everyone makes mistakes about their own birth. But {npc} remembers it, and matchmakers talk.

choices.text: Refuse politely. You are not thinking of it

effects.log: {npc} has heard that before, from everyone, and nods, and says {he} will come back in the spring. {He} does. Matchmakers always do.

choices.text: Ask about the miller's eldest. Who is this person?

effects.log: {npc} talks for an hour: the eldest is kind to animals, bad at sums, sings at the millstone. You find you have been listening with your whole self. {npc} sees it, and smiles the matchmaker's smile.

events.text: {npc} is back. The miller's family is willing. The almanac is willing. The miller's eldest, apparently, is more than willing, having seen you at the market and asked about you twice. And somewhere in the back of your mind, an old fox rule: the hundred days. A house, a person who loves the face you wear. Never let them see you sleep.

choices.text: Say yes

effects.log: {npc} claps both hands together. The red paper goes to the miller's house. You stand in your yard afterwards with your heart going like a hare's and understand that you have said yes to something you do not know how to do.

choices.text: Say no, kindly, and mean it

effects.log: {npc} sighs and takes the red paper back. "The miller's eldest will be sad," {npc} says. "So will you, I think." The matchmaker is right. Matchmakers usually are.

choices.text: Say no, and move your face to another county before they ask again

effects.log: You are gone by the next market day. The village tells it as a mystery: the quiet one who was asked to marry and vanished. The miller's eldest marries a girl from the next village in the spring, and is mostly happy.

events.text: The wedding day. A table set in the yard with a pair of wooden geese, rice, chestnuts, jujubes, a rooster and a hen tied in red and blue cloth. Half the county in the yard. The miller's eldest across the table in wedding clothes, red to the ears. And at the back of the crowd, come for the feast, an old mudang with bells at the wrist, who has stopped chatting and is looking at you over everyone's heads.

choices.text: Go through with it. Bow, and bow, and drink from the gourd

ok.log: You bow. The mudang watches the whole ceremony, the bells silent, and at the end walks up, takes your hand as if to congratulate you, and says very quietly: "Be good to that one. I will be watching." Then lets go, and goes to eat. You are in a house now. A human house, with a person in it who loves your face.

fail.log: Halfway through the bows the mudang's bells begin to ring, by themselves, louder and louder. The yard goes quiet. You finish the bows with every eye on you, and the miller's eldest holds your hand very tight under the table and says, "Ignore her. She does that at every wedding." It is not true.

choices.text: Run, before the bows. Better now than on the hundredth night

effects.log: You are over the wall in your wedding clothes and gone into the barley. Behind you the bells go silent, and somebody, the miller's eldest, is calling a name that was never yours. You hear it for a long time.

choices.text: Draw the miller's eldest aside before the ceremony and say: there are things about me you must never see

effects.log: The eldest listens, red to the ears, and laughs, and then sees your face and stops laughing. "All right," the eldest says. "I promise. I will never look." It is the first time a human has promised you anything. You do not know yet how much it weighs.

events.text: Years have gone by, one way or the other. The matchmaker is very old now and is carried round the county in a chair by grandchildren, still matching. The chair stops at your gate. "I never got it wrong," the old matchmaker says, "in sixty years. Except once, I think. A stranger at a gate, and a chart I never quite trusted. Tell me. Was I wrong?"

choices.text: "No. You were never wrong."

effects.log: The old matchmaker nods, satisfied, and taps the chair, and the grandchildren carry it on. You hear the chuckle all the way down the lane.

choices.text: "Yes. And I am glad you tried."

effects.log: "Hm," says the old matchmaker. "Everyone is glad I tried. Nobody is ever glad I was right." The chair goes on down the lane. You stand at the gate until it is out of sight.

events.text: In the next valley there is a fox who has taken the old way. You know it the way a fox knows weather: a pedlar who never came out of the pass, a funeral, another, a village that bars its gates at sunset. The hunters of the county have heard about a fox, and as far as hunters are concerned there is one fox in this county, and it lives on your hill.
events.arc: The Red Vixen of the Next Valley

choices.text: Go over the ridge and see who it is

effects.log: A sleek dark-red vixen with three tails and eyes like a hawk's, in an earth that smells of things you will not name. She is not your sister. She is something worse: a stranger who has decided. "This valley is mine," she says. "Go home, slow one."

choices.text: Move your earth further up the mountain until the hunters lose interest

effects.log: A higher earth, colder, further from everything. The hunters come to the old one, dig it out, find nothing, and go away cursing. The funerals in the next valley go on.

choices.text: Ignore it. Every fox chooses its own way

effects.log: You ignore it. The hunters do not. They come to your hill with dogs twice before the snow.

events.text: The red vixen comes to your hill herself, at midnight, and sits on your mound as if it were hers. "You smell of people," she says. "Of their bread and their lamp oil. You live among them and take nothing? That is not patience. That is cowardice with good manners." Down in your village a child is asleep with the window open.
events.arc: The Red Vixen of the Next Valley

choices.text: Fight her, here, on your own mound

ok.log: Teeth, tails, foxfire on the grass. She is faster; you are angrier. At the end she goes down the hill with one tail torn and does not come back. The funerals in the next valley stop. (-12 health)

fail.log: She is faster and older and has fed well. You end in the grass with your shoulder open, and she goes past you down into the village. In the morning the child is fine. She only wanted you to know she could. (-15 health)

choices.text: Lead the hunters to her earth tomorrow, with a trail of foxfire

effects.log: The lights go over the ridge and down into the next valley and stop over an earth that smells of the old way. The hunters dig. You do not watch. A fox does not watch another fox taken, whatever she was. The funerals stop.

choices.text: Talk. Ask her how many more she needs, and why

ok.log: "Eleven," she says, and then, slowly, the rest: a kit she lost to the dogs, a long hunger, a decision. By dawn she has not changed her mind, but she has changed valleys, going north over the mountains, far from your county. It is something.

fail.log: "Why?" she says, and laughs. "Why do you not?" She leaves at dawn. Nothing has changed except that she knows your earth now.

events.text: The county hunters come up your hill in force: twelve men, a pack of dogs, a falconer with a hawk, and a bounty from the magistrate for the fox that took the pedlar. They are certain it is you. Some of them have spoken to you, in your face, and do not know it.
events.arc: The Red Vixen of the Next Valley

choices.text: Hide the tails, keep the face, and be the helpful local when they come down tired

ok.log: They come down at dusk with nothing, and ask you for water and the road home, and curse the fox of the hill, and you give both, and agree. It is the strangest evening of your life, and not the last of its kind.

fail.log: One of the dogs will not leave your doorstep, and one of the hunters will not stop looking at it. You answer with a steady hand and do not sleep for a week.

choices.text: Lead the whole party across three ridges and lose them in the snow

ok.log: Three ridges, a frozen stream, a cliff path no dog will follow. They go home at nightfall frozen and empty-handed and tell everybody the fox of the hill is a demon. You sleep for two days.

fail.log: The hawk finds you on the second ridge, and the dogs on the third. You get away through a gully with a torn ear. (-15 health)

choices.text: Leave a sign on the hunters' path: the vixen's red fur, where she was last

effects.log: They find it, and turn their dogs to the next valley. By the first snow it is over. You do not ask how. Your hill is quiet. It does not feel clean.

events.text: Years later, a pelt in the fur trader's stall at the five-day market: dark red, three tails, very fine. The trader says it came from the north, from a vixen who took the old way in four counties before the hunters got her. People stop and stare at the tails. Children are lifted up to see. You stand in the crowd in your borrowed face.
events.arc: The Red Vixen of the Next Valley

choices.text: Buy it, with everything the face has, and bury it on the mountain

effects.log: The trader is delighted. The crowd thinks you are mad. You carry it up the mountain at night and bury it under a pine, and sit by the grave till dawn, and do not know whether you are mourning her or yourself.

choices.text: Look, and remember, and walk away

effects.log: Tails, like yours. She decided, and it went the way it always goes. You walk home the long way, past the hunters' houses, with your face held very carefully.

events.text: The first snow, and the hunters come out, the way they do every year when the snow will show them every track: falconers with hawks hooded on their gloves, beaters with long sticks, a pack of dogs, and a fur trader's promise in every pocket. Red fox pays. A fox with more than one tail, the trader said in the market, pays more than anyone in the county has ever seen. Your tracks go from the paddy to your earth as plain as writing.

choices.text: Go to ground in the earth and wait for the snow to cover your tracks

ok.log: The snow comes again at noon, thick and soft, and fills your tracks like a mother tucking in a quilt. The dogs go past your mound twice. You hear the beaters' sticks on the pines all afternoon, and then their voices going home.

fail.log: The snow stops. A dog finds the mouth of your earth and the beaters start digging. You go out through the back run with a hawk stooping at your tail. You get away. Your earth does not. (-10 health)

choices.text: Run the ridges and lay a false trail for a whole day

ok.log: Up, along, back on your own tracks, across a frozen stream where the ice will hold a fox and not a dog. By dusk the whole hunt is on the wrong mountain. You lie on a rock and watch their torches go home.

fail.log: The hawk comes down out of the white sky and the dogs are on the ridge before you can turn. You go over a cliff edge into a snowdrift, which is the only reason you are alive, and crawl home at night with the dogs baying on the wrong side of the gorge. (-15 health)

choices.text: Put on a face and walk out among them, a woodcutter coming down the hill

ok.log: "Seen any fox?" asks a falconer. "Up there," you say, pointing at the wrong mountain, "a big one." They go. The dogs whine at you all the way past. Nobody listens to a dog when a woodcutter is pointing.

fail.log: The dogs go mad at your heels and the hawk on the glove bates and screams. You walk on as fast as a woodcutter can, and the hunters watch you go, and one of them follows your tracks a long way, until they stop being a person's.

events.text: One of the hunters is good. Young, quiet, not like the others who shout: {npc}, who reads the snow the way the schoolmaster reads the classics, and goes out alone, and comes back with a red fox over the shoulder every week of the winter. Tonight {npc} is at the five-day market selling pelts, and you are walking past the stall in a face, and {npc} looks up, and looks at your feet.

choices.text: Stop at the stall and ask the price of a red pelt, coolly

ok.log: {npc} names a price. You haggle, badly, on purpose. {npc} watches your hands the whole time, but they are hands now, all the way, and at the end {npc} shrugs and goes back to the pelts. You walk away very slowly.

fail.log: You ask the price of a red pelt and your voice catches on the word. {npc} hears it. "Not for sale," {npc} says, quite gently. "Not to you."

choices.text: Walk on past, and leave the market by another road

effects.log: You do not look back. But that night, in your earth, you hear soft footsteps go past your mound in the snow, slowly, stop, and go on.

choices.text: Look at the pelts on the stall, one by one, and remember each of them

effects.log: Eleven red foxes. One with a white paw. You knew that one, a little, from the paddies. {npc} sees you looking and says, "Beautiful, aren't they?" and means it, and that is the worst of it.

events.text: At dawn, at the mouth of your earth, {npc} is kneeling in the snow with a bow across the knees, waiting. Not shooting. Just waiting, the way the good hunters wait. When you put your nose out, {npc} does not move. The two of you look at each other over ten paces of snow. Your tails are behind you, all of them, plain in the white light.

choices.text: Come out, and sit down in the snow in front of {him}

mem.note: came out and sat in front of me on the hill

effects.log: {npc} looks at the tails for a long time. Then unstrings the bow, slowly, and says, to the snow more than to you: "I knew there was something. I did not know it would be you." {He} walks away down the hill, and never hunts on it again.

choices.text: Go back down into the earth, and out the back run

ok.log: The back run is clear. You come out on the far side of the hill and look back: {npc} is still kneeling at the front, the bow across the knees, as if {he} knew you would go and wanted you to.

fail.log: {npc} has stopped the back run with a stone. You come out the front at a run and the arrow takes you across the shoulder. You are over the ridge before the second. (-14 health)

choices.text: Go at {him}, before the bow comes up

ok.log: You are on {npc} before the bow is half drawn and the bow goes into the snow, and you are gone. {npc} sits in the snow holding a bitten wrist, and laughs, shakily, the laugh of a person who has just met a story.

fail.log: {npc} was ready for that, too. A knife across your side, and you are down the hill on three legs with the blood freezing in your fur. (-15 health)

events.text: {npc} is grey now, the best hunter the county ever had, and has stopped hunting, and nobody knows why. Today {npc} brings a grandchild up your hill with a bow, a first bow, and stops at the foot of your mound, and says to the child: "Not here. Never here. Anywhere else you like. Not on this hill." The child asks why. {npc} looks at the silver grass where you are lying, and says, "Because I said so," and they go down again.

choices.text: Follow them down, unseen, as far as the village

effects.log: All the way down, a red-brown shadow in the grass beside the path. Once the grandchild turns round and stares straight at you, and {npc} puts a hand on the small shoulder and turns the child back to the road.

choices.text: Leave something on {npc}'s step that night: the first pheasant of the year

effects.log: A cock pheasant, perfect, on the step at dawn. {npc} looks at it a long time and then laughs aloud, alone, in the cold, and cooks it for the grandchild, and tells them nothing.

events.text: Every first snow now you wake before dawn and lie in the earth listening, and you can tell from the sound of the dogs, two ridges off, how many there are and how hungry, and from the sound of the hawks whether the falconers are young. A fox who has lived through enough first snows learns to read them the way people read the almanac.

choices.text: Teach the young foxes of the hill what you know

effects.log: The young field foxes of the valley come to your mound in autumn, nervous, and you teach them: the frozen stream, the back run, the dog who is old and the dog who is not. Some of them listen. Some of them always live through the winter.

choices.text: Keep it to yourself. Every fox learns it alone

effects.log: You read the snow, and survive it, alone. It is how you learned. It is how foxes have always learned, which is why so few of them get old.

events.text: At the temple on the next mountain a boy of twelve studies with an old monk: a farmer's son, they say, who taught himself the calendar by watching the sun on the wall. You have been past the temple many times. Today a stranger rides up to the gate on a small donkey, attended by two boys in blue, and says he has come from Mount Taebaek, and asks to test the boy on the classics. The wind changes. You smell what the stranger is: a fox, nine tails, so old the smell is like dust in a tomb. It has not come for the classics.

choices.text: Put on a face, find the old monk, and warn the temple

ok.log: The old monk hears you out and nods, unsurprised. "I know," the monk says. "I have known for three days. But thank you. It is good to know the mountain has friends." The monk looks at your face, and then at your shadow, and smiles. "Several kinds of friends."

fail.log: The old monk looks at you for a long time, then says: "You are one of them." Then, more gently: "But not that one. Go home, little one. This is too old for you." You go. You do not go far.

choices.text: Go to the stranger yourself, fox to fox, and ask what it wants

ok.log: The stranger looks down at you from the donkey with eyes like old bronze. "The brightest one in a thousand years," it says. "You would do the same, at nine tails." It rides on. You are shaking so hard you cannot stand for an hour.

fail.log: The stranger looks at you, once. That is all. You wake at dusk in a ditch a mile away with your ears ringing and blood in your nose, and do not know how you got there. (-18 health)

choices.text: Watch from the hill. Nine tails is nine tails

effects.log: You watch the stranger test the boy all afternoon, and the boy answer everything, and the stranger smile. Then the stranger rides away down the valley, slowly, as if it had all the time in the world, and it does.

events.text: The old monk does not sleep for three days, sitting in meditation. On the fourth, before dawn, the monk takes the boy by the hand and goes west, fast, faster than an old monk walks, and you follow the scent of them for days: to a mountaintop where an ancient tree stands alone. The monk cuts five pieces of wood from it and sits carving, and painting each figure a colour: blue, white, red, black, and yellow.

choices.text: Bring the monk water and keep watch while the carving goes on

effects.log: Three days of carving. You bring water in your mouth from the spring below, a little at a time, and lie at the edge of the clearing at night with your ears up. On the third day the monk says, without looking up, "Thank you, fox." The boy stares at you all the way home.

choices.text: Breathe a little of the bead's light into the yellow figure

effects.log: While the monk sleeps, you breathe on the yellow figure, the last. The paint glows for a moment like a lamp behind paper and then goes ordinary. In the morning the monk looks at it, and then at you, for a long time, and says nothing.

choices.text: Go home. This is a monk's fight, and the stranger knows your scent

effects.log: You turn back at the foot of the mountain. Behind you the knock of a carving knife goes on all night.

events.text: Dusk, the village below the temple, and a commotion at the village entrance that the villagers will talk about for centuries. Five carved figures stand in the road in a row, and something comes down the valley that is not a stranger on a donkey any more. The blue figure goes down. The white. The red. The black. The yellow stands alone in the road with the dark coming at it, and dawn is still an hour away.

choices.text: Stand beside the yellow guardian

ok.log: An hour of it, a fox of three or four tails beside a carved wooden figure, against something with nine. Your foxfire, its foxfire, the yellow paint, the dawn. The sun comes up. You are lying in the road beside the yellow figure, and you are alive, and something else is not. (-25 health)

fail.deathCause: the old fox from Mount Taebaek
fail.log: It is too old, and you are too young, and the yellow figure is too far away. It throws you into the ditch the way a cat throws a mouse it has decided not to eat, and goes on. You wake at noon in the cold water with a torn ear, alive because you were not worth the time. (-20 health)

choices.text: Lead it astray with foxfire, off the road and round the hill, until dawn comes

ok.log: It knows every trick you know and a thousand more. But it is hungry, and in a hurry, and your lights are very good. Round the hill, round again, and the sky goes grey. The yellow figure is waiting in the road when it comes back. It does not leave the road again.

fail.log: It laughs at your lights and swats you into a paddy as it passes. You lie in the cold water and hear the last of the fight at the village entrance, and the cock crow, and then a silence. (-15 health)

choices.text: Watch from the hill, and pray to the yellow figure as if it were a god

effects.log: You have never prayed. You do now, for an hour, to a piece of painted wood. At dawn the yellow figure is still standing. You do not know whether it heard you. You decide it did.

events.text: In the morning there is an old fox lying dead in the road at the village entrance, with nine tails, smaller than anyone expected, and five carved figures standing round it, four of them split. The boy stands at the edge of the crowd looking at it. Years later that boy will be the scholar the whole country calls Hwadam, the Flower Pool, and will never tell anyone what happened at the village entrance when he was twelve.

choices.text: Go and look at the dead fox, close

effects.log: Nine tails. Grey at the roots. A face like any old fox's. You stand over it a long time, and the villagers do not even notice one more fox in the crowd. That is what nine tails looks like, at the end of the old way. You go home and bow to the moon until morning.

choices.text: Watch the boy, and remember the face

effects.log: The boy looks up from the dead fox and straight at you, across the crowd, at the fox sitting in the grass by the road. A long look. Then the boy bows, very slightly, the way a monk bows. Of course the boy knows. The boy knows everything.

events.text: The third tail comes in with the autumn, and you feel it the way a person feels a new tooth: all the time, and with your tongue. In a face you hold it in. It is like holding your breath. Tonight in the back room, alone, with the lamp lit, you let it go for a moment, and look at the wall, and there are three tails on the paper door, enormous, waving like reeds.
events.arc: The Tails That Will Not Hide

choices.text: Practise in front of the lamp every night until the shadow behaves

ok.log: A month of nights in front of a lamp. By the end the shadow is a person's from the front, the side, the back. Only when you laugh, sometimes, a tail comes back into it. You learn not to laugh near lamps.

fail.log: The tails go into the shadow and come back out of it like children who will not stay in bed. One night you hear a footstep in the yard and blow the lamp out so fast you burn your fingers.

choices.text: Never light a lamp in a room you are in again

effects.log: A whole new way of living: in the dark, by moonlight, by the light of other people's lamps through doors. People start to call your face thrifty. It is the best thing they could call it.

choices.text: Go out to the mound and let all three tails go, in the open, under the moon

effects.log: All three, fanned out on the grass, the moon on them. You had forgotten what it feels like to be all of yourself at once. A farmer on the hill road sees it from far off, and tells the village there is a fox with three tails on the grave mounds, and nobody believes the farmer.

events.text: The fourth tail, and it will not stay folded. It is restless, like the bead: it wants out at dusk, at the full moon, when a dog barks. Tonight a girl from the next house comes in without knocking, the way neighbours do, with a bowl of soup, and the lamp is lit, and you are bent over the stove with your back to the paper door, and she looks at the door, and the bowl hits the floor, and she screams.
events.arc: The Tails That Will Not Hide

choices.text: Turn round smiling, the face all there, and ask what is the matter

ok.log: "A shadow," she says, "behind you, with...", and looks again, and the shadow on the door is a person bent over a stove. She laughs, shakily, and apologises, and you help her pick up the bowl. She does not come in without knocking again.

fail.log: You turn too fast. One tail comes round with you. She runs. By morning half the street has heard the story and the other half is pretending not to have. You sit in the dark with the lamp out and listen to the dogs.

choices.text: Blow out the lamp, and in the dark say quietly: "It was the smoke"

effects.log: In the dark, nothing can be seen, and so nothing was. She stands there breathing hard, then says, "The smoke," in a small voice, and goes home, and lies awake. So do you.

choices.text: Let her look. Let the tails be seen once, and see what happens

effects.log: Four tails, in the lamplight, in a kitchen. She stops screaming. She looks for a long time, and then she says, "Oh," quite softly, and puts the soup down on the stove, and goes home, and does not tell anyone for three days. Then she does.

events.text: Four tails. Behind you on the mound at night they lie fanned on the frost like the spokes of a wheel. A fox with four tails is a fox the stories have a name for, and the villages tell those stories to their children with the doors barred. Every tail is a hundred years and a little more strength, and every tail is one more thing to hide.
events.arc: The Tails That Will Not Hide

choices.text: Count what you have hidden this century, and what it cost

effects.log: A face, a name, a shadow, a laugh. The cost is a tiredness that does not go away with sleep. You fold the four tails round your feet and decide that you will spend it, all of it, on purpose.

choices.text: Bow to the moon all night with all four tails open

effects.log: The whole mound glows faintly. The bead takes in the moon like a dry field takes rain. In the village below a dog howls once and then thinks better of it.

events.text: Six bandits from the hills at your gate at midnight, with clubs, a rusty sword and a very confident leader, {npc}, who wants the jars, the coins under the floor, and a promise of the same every new moon. The regulars have gone very quiet behind you. The leader smiles. "A keeper alone," {npc} says, "at a crossroads. You should be grateful we are the first."

choices.text: Pay them, this once, and remember every face

effects.log: They take two jars and go, laughing. You remember six faces and six smells. The next new moon, six bandits wake up in six different paddies, up to the chest, with no idea how they got there. The new moon after that, they do not come.

choices.text: Smile back, and fight them in the gateway

ok.log: A keeper with a ladle against six clubs. The ladle wins. The regulars talk about it for years, and the more they talk the faster you were, until you are moving like something that is not a person at all. Which you were.

fail.log: Two of them, you put down. The third gets you with the club across the ribs. The regulars pile in then, and the bandits go, and you are in bed for a month being nursed by a ferryman. (-15 health)

choices.text: Lead them off with foxfire: lights in the reeds, like a treasure lantern

effects.log: A light in the reeds, swinging like a lantern on a pole: somebody running away with something. The bandits go after it. They follow it until dawn, round the marsh, and come back out where they started, wet and cursing, and the keeper is serving breakfast.

events.text: Word comes in with a carter: bandits waiting at the bend below the pass for the salt cart that left your yard at dawn. The salt carter is a regular, old, and has a grandchild riding on the sacks today. The bend is a morning's walk for a person. For a fox it is a short run over the ridge.

choices.text: Run the ridge as a fox and get there first

ok.log: You are at the bend before the cart. Foxfire in the trees above the bandits, voices in the rocks, a laugh that comes from everywhere: they break and run uphill. The cart comes round the bend an hour later. The grandchild waves at a fox on a rock.

fail.log: You arrive with the cart. The bandits are at it already. You come down out of the trees snarling and the oxen bolt and the bandits scatter and the salt goes everywhere. Nobody is hurt but you. (-8 health)

choices.text: Send a regular to warn the carter on the main road, and stay in the face

effects.log: A regular's boy runs it. The salt cart waits at the inn below for a convoy. Nobody is robbed and nobody sees anything a keeper should not do. It is less satisfying. It is much safer.

events.text: The bandit leader {npc} comes back, alone, years later, without a club: thinner, a beggar now, with a limp. {npc} stands at the gate and does not come in. "Six of us came to your gate once, and nothing after it went the way it should have," {npc} says. "I have thought about it for years. I would like a bowl, and to know what you are."

choices.text: Pour the bowl, and tell {him}

mem.note: told me the truth at the crossroads and poured me a bowl

effects.log: {npc} drinks the bowl in one go, and listens, and nods, and laughs, a long tired laugh. "I knew it was not a person," {he} says. "No person is that patient." {He} sleeps in your stable and leaves at dawn, and you hear later {he} works the ferry and never steals again.

choices.text: Pour the bowl, and say only: a keeper who does not like bandits

effects.log: {npc} drinks, and looks at you, and shrugs. "Fair," {he} says. "Fair." {He} goes, limping. It is enough of an answer, for a bandit.

choices.text: Close the gate

effects.log: The gate closes. {npc} stands outside it a while. In the morning {he} is gone, and there is a knife stuck in your gatepost, handle-first, as if offered.

events.text: A widow from the village, {npc}, poor, in white hemp that has been mended many times, comes to your mound at dusk with a little plate of rice cakes. Not for the grave: the grave is not {his} family's. "For the stray," {npc} says to the grass. "I have seen you on the hill. You are thin. My child was thin, too, before the fever." {He} sets the plate down and goes away without looking back.

choices.text: Eat the rice cakes when {he} has gone

effects.log: Sticky, sweet, with a bean paste that tastes of somebody's kitchen. You eat every one and lick the plate. In the morning the plate is gone: {npc} came back for it before dawn, and smiled at the clean plate, and you saw.

choices.text: Come out of the grass and eat them while {he} is still there

mem.note: ate my rice cakes in front of me

effects.log: {npc} stands very still. You eat. {He} crouches down slowly, a little way off, and watches, and tells you about {his} child, the whole story, while the light goes. You listen to all of it. Nobody else in the village ever did.

choices.text: Leave them for the crows. You do not need a widow's charity

effects.log: The crows eat them. {npc} comes back for the plate the next morning and finds it pecked clean, and is pleased anyway, and comes back at Chuseok with more.

events.text: Every Chuseok for years, the widow {npc} brings the rice cakes up the hill, and sits a while, and talks: the price of salt, a neighbour's wedding, the roof. You have stopped hiding in the grass. You sit on the next mound and listen. {He} calls you "the stray" still, and it has become a name.

choices.text: Bring {him} something back: a pheasant, left on the step

effects.log: Every Chuseok after, a pheasant on the widow's step the next morning. {npc} tells the village a fox brings it, and the village laughs, and {npc} eats well all autumn and does not care who laughs.

choices.text: Mend {his} roof one night, quietly, in a face

ok.log: New thatch over the leak by morning. {npc} stands in the yard looking up at it with both hands over {his} mouth. The village says the stray must have done it, and laughs again. {npc} does not laugh.

fail.log: You fall through the roof into the kitchen in the middle of the night, in a face, with an armful of straw. {npc} sits up on the mat and looks at you a long time, and says, "Well. Fix it, then," and goes back to sleep.

events.text: {npc} is very old now, alone in the cold house at the end of the village, and this winter {he} does not come up the hill. You go down. Through the paper of the window you hear {him} talking, the way the old talk to the dead: to {his} child, the one who died of the fever, telling the child to come home, it is getting dark. A face would be easy. The child's face. You remember it from {his} stories better than anyone alive.

choices.text: Put on the lost child's face, grown up, and go in, and stay the winter

mem.note: sent my child home for the last winter

effects.log: {npc} looks up from the mat and says the child's name, and holds out both hands. You stay all winter: the fire, the gruel, the stories {he} has told you a hundred times, told to you again as if new. It is the kindest lie you have ever told. You are not sure it is a lie.

choices.text: Go in as a stranger, a neighbour, and keep {him} warm

effects.log: A neighbour {he} does not quite remember, who brings wood and stays. {npc} talks to you about the stray on the hill, who is very thin, and asks you to take it rice cakes. You promise.

choices.text: Lend the bead for a night, on your breath, so {he} is warm until spring

ok.log: The bead goes on a breath and comes back at dawn, dim and warm. {npc} wakes warm all through for the first time in years, and gets up, and makes rice cakes, and takes them up the hill, slowly, to the stray. You eat every one. (Lent, and returned)

fail.log: The bead goes on a breath, and the old one swallows in sleep, the way the old swallow medicine. In the morning {npc} is warm, and looking at the ground as if the floor had become a window. The bead does not come back. A tail folds.

events.text: The widow {npc} dies in the spring, in {his} sleep, with the window open toward the hill. The village buries {him} on the slope below your mound, because nobody else has a place for {him}, and nobody brings rice cakes, because there is nobody left who would.

choices.text: Bring rice cakes to the grave every Chuseok, in a face, for as long as there are Chuseoks

effects.npcPass: old age, in spring, in sleep, with the window open toward the hill
effects.log: Every year, a stranger in plain clothes with a little plate. The village decides it must be a relative from far away. For generations the stranger never misses one, and never looks a day older, and the village decides that is a relative too.

choices.text: Sit on the grave on the night after the funeral, as a fox, and do not move till dawn

effects.npcPass: old age, in spring, in sleep, with the window open toward the hill
effects.log: The village sees a fox on the widow's grave all night and says the stray came to mourn. They are right. It is the first time the village has been right about you, and it is about the only thing you would want them to be right about.

events.text: A child of the house next to yours, {npc}, has had a fever for nine days that the physician cannot break. The physician has gone home and said, in the yard, the thing physicians say when they mean they have stopped. The child's parents sit up in turns. And your bead, after centuries of moonlight, is finally bright enough to do what the old foxes say a bead can do.

choices.text: Go in at night and let the bead pass on your breath to the child

ok.log: The parent asleep against the wall does not wake. The bead goes across, small and bright, and in the grey before dawn it comes back to you, and the child is sweating, and cool, and asleep properly for the first time in nine days. You go home and sit in the dark and shake. It came back. (Lent, and returned)

fail.log: The bead goes across on a breath, and the child, half waking, swallows it the way a sick child swallows medicine, all at once. The fever breaks by morning. The bead does not come back. Half your light is in a five-year-old now, and a tail folds against your back.

choices.text: Bring the parents willow bark and honey from the hills, and keep the bead

effects.log: It helps, a little. The fever goes on another week and breaks by itself. The child lives. You will never know whether the bead would have been faster, and you will think about it for a long time.

choices.text: Stay away. A bead in a child's mouth is a bead that may not come back

effects.log: You stay in. All night you hear the parents moving in the next house. At dawn the fever breaks on its own, and you are so relieved that you are ashamed of it.

events.text: The child {npc} is well, and has decided that you are the most interesting person on the street, and follows you to the well, the market, the woodpile, asking questions. Today the question is: "Why do your eyes go gold in the dark? Mine don't."

choices.text: "Because I eat my carrots."

ok.log: {npc} looks at you with deep suspicion, and eats carrots for a year, and checks in a basin of water every night. You never laugh in front of the child. You laugh a great deal elsewhere.

fail.log: "That is a lie," says {npc}, very pleased. "Grown-ups always say carrots." {He} tells the whole street you have gold eyes and lie about carrots. The street laughs. Mostly.

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth, as a secret between the two of you

mem.note: saved me, and the neighbour told me you were a fox

effects.log: {npc} listens with enormous eyes and keeps the secret, completely, for the rest of {his} life, which is a thing children are better at than anyone believes.

events.text: {npc}, the child of the fever, is grown now, with a house and a cough-prone child of {his} own, and comes to your door one night with the child in {his} arms and the fever in the child's face, and does not explain anything. {He} just holds the child out to you.

choices.text: Take the child, and let the bead pass on your breath again

ok.log: The bead goes, and comes back. The grandchild of the fever sleeps cool by morning. {npc} takes the child home without a word and leaves on your step a pair of new straw sandals, exactly your size. (Lent, and returned)

fail.log: The bead goes, and the small one swallows. {npc} looks at you over the child's head, understanding all at once what it cost, and says, "I will bring it back. I swear it." A tail folds.

choices.text: Give herbs and advice, and say the bead is not yours to give twice

effects.log: {npc} nods, as if {he} expected that, and thanks you, and goes home and does exactly what you said. The child lives. Most children do, with care. You stand at the door a long time.

events.text: A stranger comes in out of the dusk: very tall, very quiet, barefoot, with white hair though the face is not old, in a grey hemp coat that smells of pine resin and snow and something underneath that makes every hair on your back rise. {npc} sits in the corner, drinks three bowls, and says nothing to anyone. In the morning there is a whole deer at your kitchen door, still warm, and the stranger is gone.
events.arc: The Guest Who Is Not a Guest

choices.text: Keep the deer, and pour three bowls for the corner when {he} comes again

effects.log: {npc} comes again at the next full moon, and finds three bowls already poured in the corner, and stops in the doorway. Then sits, and drinks them. And looks at you, once, the way one great beast looks at another across a river.

choices.text: Go up the mountain at dawn, as a fox, and follow the tracks

ok.log: Bare human footprints in the frost, going up the pass, and then, where the pines close, not human footprints at all: round, wide, deep, the size of a rice bowl. You turn round very quietly and go home.

fail.log: You follow the tracks too far. Something on the rocks above you coughs, once, a deep sound, and you are halfway down the mountain before you have decided to run. (-10 health)

events.text: Closing time, and the white-haired guest {npc} is the last one at the tables. {He} looks at you over the bowl and says, in a voice that is mostly a rumble: "Fox." Not a question. "Your tails show on the door when you laugh. Do not worry. They see only what they want to see." {He} drinks. "Mine show on the wall when I am hungry."
events.arc: The Guest Who Is Not a Guest

choices.text: "Then do not be hungry in my house."

effects.log: A sound like a landslide: {npc} is laughing. "Fair," {he} says. "Fair, fox." {He} is never hungry in your house. Nobody on that road is ever taken by the tiger of the pass while you keep the crossroads.

choices.text: Ask {him} why a great beast drinks with humans at all

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it, longer than you expected. "To remember what I am guarding," {he} says. "And you, fox? Why do you pour for them?" You do not have an answer. {He} nods, as if that were one.

choices.text: Say nothing, and wipe the table, with your back to {him}

effects.log: You wipe the table. The guest leaves the bowl and goes. On the wall where the lamp was, for a moment, there are stripes. You decide not to have seen them, which is a courtesy between beasts.

events.text: Tiger-catching soldiers in your yard: the governor's men, with spears and nets and a sergeant who has hunted tigers in four provinces. A tiger has been seen on the pass. They want to know who comes down from the mountain, who pays in game, who sits in the corner. The regulars look at the corner. It is empty tonight. Three bowls are poured there.
events.arc: The Guest Who Is Not a Guest

choices.text: Tell them the corner is for the dead: a custom of the house

ok.log: The sergeant takes off his helmet to the corner, respectfully, and the soldiers go up the wrong mountain in the morning. Three days later there is a deer at your kitchen door, and the three bowls are empty.

fail.log: The sergeant looks at the corner, and at you, and at the deer antlers over your door, and writes something down. The soldiers stay a week. The corner stays empty. You are watched as well.

choices.text: Go up the pass that night, as a fox, and warn the guest

ok.log: You find a white shape in the snow above the pass that you are very careful not to look at directly, and you say, "Soldiers. Nets. The east side." A rumble in the dark. In the morning the soldiers find nothing, and so do you, ever, but the deer keep coming.

fail.log: You run straight into a soldiers' net on the pass. You chew your way out by dawn, and the sergeant finds the net in the morning, chewed, and red-brown hair in it, and frowns. (-12 health)

choices.text: Tell the soldiers nothing at all, and pour them nothing either

effects.log: A keeper who will not pour for the governor's men is a keeper who gets remembered. You do not care. The soldiers drink elsewhere and catch nothing.

events.text: The white-haired guest {npc} comes in one last time, in the first snow, and does not sit. "The mountain needs me," {he} says. "Higher up. I will not be on this pass again in your life, fox, or I think in mine." {He} puts down on the table, between the bowls, a single white hair, as long as your forearm, with a black stripe across it.
events.arc: The Guest Who Is Not a Guest

choices.text: Give {him} a hair of your own in return: red-brown, from the tip of a tail

effects.log: {npc} takes it between two enormous fingers and looks at it a long time, and puts it inside the coat. "Pour well," {he} says, and goes up into the snow. Behind you, years later, other beasts will tell each other about a fox and a tiger who drank together, and get the story wrong.

choices.text: Pour the three bowls one last time, and drink one yourself

effects.log: Three bowls, two beasts, one table. Neither of you says anything. At the end {npc} bows, the way a guest bows, and goes. You keep the white hair in the ledger, between the pages for that year.

events.text: Your salt-fish stall at the river market, and a quarrel at the next one: {npc}, a farmer's widow, swears the fish bought there weighed less at home than on the stall. The stall-keeper swears by the ancestors. Your fox's nose tells you the stall-keeper's scale has a lump of wet clay under the pan. Nobody has asked you anything.
events.arc: A Year in a Borrowed Face

choices.text: Lean over and lift the pan, so everybody sees the clay

mem.note: showed up the cheat who sold me short

effects.log: The clay falls on the board with a wet slap. The market laughs. {npc} gets the right weight and a free fish, and buys from your stall forever after. The cheat moves to another market and tells everyone you have the eyes of a cat.

choices.text: Quietly sell {npc} a fish at your stall for the difference

effects.log: {npc} takes it, puzzled and grateful. The cheat goes on cheating. You have not made an enemy, and you have not made anything right. It is a very human compromise, and you notice that you are good at it.

choices.text: Mind your own stall. A fox who notices too much gets noticed

effects.log: You sell fish and look at the river. {npc} goes home short-weighted and furious. You have learned the first rule of the market, which is the same as the first rule of the hill.

events.text: A salt peddler stops at your fish stall: {npc}, a big slow person with a pole across the shoulders, two heavy baskets of grey sea salt, and a stick for walking that is worn black at the top. {npc} buys nothing. {npc} just stands at the stall looking at you, then at the stick, then at you, the way the vixen who raised you taught you never to let a salt peddler look.
events.arc: A Year in a Borrowed Face

choices.text: Offer the best fish on the stall, cheap, and keep talking

ok.log: You talk about salt, weather, the price of rope. {npc} buys the fish, and thanks you, and says, as the pole goes back on the shoulders: "You keep a good stall, for somebody from so far off." Then walks on. You sell nothing else all afternoon. Your hands will not stop shaking.

fail.log: The stick comes up and down on the stall board between you, quite gently, as if testing it, and your face slips at the edges like a reflection when a stone goes in. {npc} nods slowly. "I thought so," {npc} says. You leave the stall and the fish and the town before dark. (-5 health)

choices.text: Pack up the stall and go, now, before the stick moves

effects.log: You leave half the fish on the board. {npc} watches you go without moving. Behind you, you hear the slow voice say to the next stall, "Funny. They always run."

choices.text: Look straight back at {npc}, and say: "I have harmed nobody in this town"

mem.note: looked me in the eye at the fish stall

effects.log: {npc} considers it for a long time, leaning on the stick. "So far," {npc} says at last, and walks on with the salt. It is not a pardon. It is a warning, and a kind of respect.

events.text: Your pedlar's pack, at a farmhouse gate in the hills: needles, thread, combs, a little mirror. The daughter of the house, {npc}, buys three needles, and then, embarrassed, holds out a letter. From a brother at the northern frontier, a year old. Nobody in the house can read. Would the pedlar?
events.arc: A Year in a Borrowed Face

choices.text: Read it aloud, every word, exactly as written

mem.note: read me my brother's letter

effects.log: The brother is cold, and well, and misses the persimmons. {npc} cries, and laughs, and makes you read it twice more. You leave with no money for the needles and an armful of persimmons, and go back every spring to read the new one.

choices.text: Read it aloud, and make it a little warmer than it is

ok.log: The letter is short and tired. In your mouth it is longer, and asks after everyone by name. {npc} hears it and glows. It is a lie, and the kind of lie you are best at, and you are not sure you are sorry.

fail.log: You warm it up and {npc} frowns: the brother never called anybody "dearest" in a whole life. You fumble it back. {npc} looks at you strangely, and pays for the needles in full.

choices.text: Say you cannot read either, and move on

effects.log: A pedlar who reads is a pedlar who is remembered. You move on. Behind you {npc} stands at the gate with the letter in both hands.

events.text: On the county road a pedlar of the big guild, {npc}, falls into step beside you with a pack twice the size of yours and a guild tally hanging from the hat. Guild pedlars look after each other, {npc} explains: inns, news, who to avoid. Of course, a member needs a home county, a sponsor, and a name in the guild book. "Where are you from, friend?"
events.arc: A Year in a Borrowed Face

choices.text: Invent a county and a sponsor, and join

ok.log: A county far enough off, a sponsor conveniently dead. Your name goes in the guild book in good ink. For decades after, you are fed at guild inns from one end of the province to the other, and you hear every rumour in the country, including a great many about foxes.

fail.log: {npc} knows the county you invent: was born there, in fact. "Funny," {npc} says, "I never saw you." You laugh, and part at the next crossroads, and {npc} tells the next inn about the pedlar from nowhere.

choices.text: Thank {npc}, and say you walk alone

effects.log: "Suit yourself," says {npc}, without offence. They always say that. You walk alone, which you are good at, and which is beginning to feel like a smaller thing than it did.

events.text: A young soldier, {npc}, on the way north to the frontier fort, sits at your counter long after the others have gone, turning the bowl round and round. Seventeen, perhaps. Not drinking. "Keeper," {npc} says at last, "have you ever been very far from home, and afraid you would never see it again?"
events.arc: A Year in a Borrowed Face

choices.text: "Yes." And tell {npc} about it, without saying what you are

mem.note: talked to me all night at the crossroads before I went north

effects.log: You tell it as if it were a human story: the earth, the mother who did not come back, the long road. {npc} listens till the lamp gutters. In the morning {npc} goes north with a lighter pack. Seven years later a soldier stops at the crossroads on the way home, and asks for the keeper.

choices.text: Pour {npc} a bowl on the house, and say every soldier is afraid

effects.log: {npc} drinks it, and laughs, and is a little less afraid, which is all a bowl can do. You stand in the gate at dawn and watch the road north until it is empty.

choices.text: The breath of the frightened is warm. Wait until {npc} sleeps in the back room

effects.log: In the back room, at the end of the night, a thread of breath from a frightened young sleeper. The bead glows. In the morning {npc} goes north pale and stumbling, and you wave from the gate. (+1 Breath debt)

events.text: {npc}, a rich landlord's steward, very drunk, has decided that the keeper's face is the funniest thing on the salt road, and is saying so, loudly, to the whole room: the eyes, too narrow, "like a fox's, ha", the way you walk, the way you never eat in front of anyone. The room is laughing uneasily. {npc} is going to sleep it off in your back room, and nobody would miss a little colour in a face like that.
events.arc: A Year in a Borrowed Face

choices.text: Laugh along. Pour {npc} another, and let it go

effects.log: You laugh, and pour, and agree your eyes are very narrow. {npc} falls asleep on the bench mid-joke. The room relaxes. In the morning {npc} remembers nothing, and pays double from embarrassment.

choices.text: Take the breath, in the back room, while {npc} snores

effects.log: Nobody would miss it, and nobody does, except {npc}, who wakes up grey and sick and blames the drink, and never comes back to the crossroads, and never says anything about foxes again. (+1 Breath debt)

choices.text: Throw {npc} out into the road, with a ladle

ok.log: Out, and the gate shut. The room cheers. The story goes round three counties as the night the keeper threw the steward over the wall, and by the time it comes back the steward has been thrown over a house.

fail.log: The steward is heavier than a deer. You get {npc} as far as the gate, where both of you fall over, and the room laughs at both of you equally, which is better than what it was laughing at before.

events.text: A poetry gathering in a pavilion by the river, in your face as a scholar between examinations. Somebody recites a famous old poem about the moon on grave mounds, a poem the whole county knows, author unknown, a hundred years old. {npc}, a sharp-eyed rival, leans over and murmurs, "Your style is very like it. Suspiciously like it." You wrote it. You wrote it on a temple wall in a different face, a century ago.
events.arc: A Year in a Borrowed Face

choices.text: Say nothing, and let the poem stay unknown

effects.log: The poem goes on being nobody's, which is the safest thing a poem can be. You write a worse one that afternoon, on purpose, and {npc} relaxes and calls you derivative. You will take derivative.

choices.text: Recite the second half, which nobody has heard, because it was never written down

effects.log: The pavilion goes silent. Four new lines, and the old poem is suddenly whole, and better. {npc} stares at you. Somebody writes it down. By autumn the county says the poem was found, and argues about how, and you are invited to every gathering for years.

choices.text: Turn it on {npc}: "Like it? I wish I could write like that."

ok.log: {npc} preens. The suspicion goes out of the murmur like air from a bellows. It is easy to make a rival forget a question by giving a rival a compliment.

fail.log: "Do you?" says {npc}. "I would have said you could." The rival keeps an eye on you all afternoon.

events.text: {npc}, a younger scholar from the village, has asked you to tutor {him} for the county examination: you, the quiet scholar who never seems to study and always seems to know. Evenings at your low table, {npc} reciting, you correcting. Tonight {npc} falls asleep over the book, head on the table, breathing slow and warm.
events.arc: A Year in a Borrowed Face

choices.text: Put a quilt over {him} and keep reading alone

mem.note: let me sleep through lessons and never said a word

effects.log: You read till dawn, by moonlight, so as not to light a lamp. {npc} wakes with the quilt round {him} and looks at you, embarrassed and grateful. {He} passes the examination that spring, third in the county.

choices.text: A thread of breath. Just one. The bead is so close to the next tail

effects.log: One thread of breath, and the bead glows. {npc} wakes with a headache and studies badly for a month and fails the examination by one place. You correct {his} essays more kindly after that, and are not forgiven by yourself. (+1 Breath debt)

choices.text: Wake {him} gently and send {him} home to sleep in a proper bed

effects.log: "Go home," you say. "Sleep. A tired head learns nothing." {npc} goes, yawning. You sit alone at the table with the warm place where {his} breath was, and look at it, and then put out the lamp.

events.text: Your herb stall's waiting room is full of the poor, as it always is: a cough, a burn, a child with worms, a farmhand with a cut gone bad. Into the middle of it walks {npc}, steward to the county's richest family, in silk, who says the master of the house has a headache and you are to come at once, and the others can wait.
events.arc: A Year in a Borrowed Face

choices.text: Say the others came first, and the master can come and wait too

effects.log: The waiting room goes very quiet and then, all at once, very approving. {npc} goes red and leaves. The next day the master of the house comes in person, with a headache, and sits on the bench between a farmhand and a goat, and waits.

choices.text: Go. The rich pay, and the money will buy medicine for the poor

effects.log: You go. The headache is wine. You charge the price of medicine for the whole waiting room, and get it, and come back at dusk to find them all still sitting there, patient as cattle. You work till midnight.

choices.text: Send {npc} back with willow bark and a message: drink less

effects.log: {npc} takes it back. The master of the house laughs, and drinks less, and sends a sack of rice to your stall with no message at all.

events.text: {npc} comes to your herb stall pale. Not the pallor of fever: the moonlight pallor of a sleeper who has lost breath in the night, the kind you know better than any physician alive. You did not do this. Somewhere in this town there is another fox.
events.arc: A Year in a Borrowed Face

choices.text: Treat {npc} as best a human physician could, and say nothing

effects.log: Ginseng, rest, a dog in the room at night. {npc} recovers, slowly. You walk the town that night with your nose up and find nothing but a scent on the wind, old and faintly amused.

choices.text: Lend the bead to {npc} for a night: a breath given back, even if not yours

ok.log: The bead goes and comes back. In the morning {npc} has colour. It was not your debt, and it feels exactly the same to pay it. (Lent, and returned)

fail.log: The bead goes, and {npc}, frightened in the dark, swallows. Half your light is gone into a stranger who was paying someone else's debt. A tail folds.

choices.text: Hunt for the other fox

ok.log: Under the floor of the magistrate's storehouse: a young fox, one tail, half-starved and terrified. You chase it out of the county with a lecture it will remember for a century. The pale ones of the town get their colour back by spring.

fail.log: You find nothing, except that the town watchman finds you, at midnight, sniffing at a storehouse floor, and asks what an herb physician wants there. Herbs, you say. The watchman does not believe you.

events.text: In the temple's grey as a novice, sweeping the yard at dawn. The temple dog hates you, quietly and permanently. Today a pilgrim, {npc}, an old farmer who walked three days, sits on the step and tells you, because you are only a novice and novices do not count, that {his} son is a thief, and {he} has come to pray that the son is caught, before the son does worse.
events.arc: A Year in a Borrowed Face

choices.text: Listen, and sweep, and say the prayer with {him}

effects.log: You say it together on the step. You do not know if it is a good prayer. {npc} goes home lighter. In the autumn the son is caught for a small theft, and flogged, and comes home, and does not steal again. Prayers work, sometimes, in the way they would least like to.

choices.text: Tell {him} the abbot is wiser, and fetch the abbot

effects.log: The abbot comes and says the right things. {npc} is grateful. The abbot looks at you afterward, the novice who never eats in the refectory, and says only: "You listen well. Sweep the east yard too."

choices.text: Go and find the son yourself that night, as a fox, and frighten {him} straight

effects.log: Foxfire round a thief's camp in the hills, and a voice from the dark that knows the thief's mother's name. The son is home within the week, swearing off everything. {npc} comes back to the temple to give thanks, and gives them to the wrong god.

events.text: The dawn chant at the temple: forty monks, the great bell, the wooden fish, the long sutra. You stand in the back row in your grey. Every morning the chant pulls at your face like a current. This morning the novice next to you, {npc}, a sharp-eyed youngster of the village who came for a year, is staring at your ears.
events.arc: A Year in a Borrowed Face

choices.text: Chant louder. Hold the face with the chant itself

ok.log: You stop fighting the chant and ride it. The face settles like silt in a jar. {npc} looks at your ears, which are ordinary, and frowns at {his} own eyes. By the end of the year you can chant the whole sutra without a hair moving, and {npc} has decided {he} imagined it.

fail.log: An ear goes up. You put it down. {npc} sees. After the chant {npc} follows you to the well, and stands there, and says nothing, and fills {his} bucket, and goes. Every morning after, {npc} chants next to you, watching.

choices.text: Slip out of the hall, as if ill

effects.log: Outside in the cold you lean on a pillar and wait for your ears. {npc} comes out after the chant and asks, kindly, if you are better. You say yes. {npc} says, kindly, that {he} will chant for your health. You beg {him} not to.

choices.text: Look back at {npc}, and wink

effects.log: {npc} nearly drops the prayer beads. Then, slowly, {npc} smiles, and looks to the front, and chants the rest of the sutra with great seriousness. The two of you are friends for {his} whole year at the temple, and {he} never says a word to anyone.

events.text: Market gossip at the well, in your face, with a jar on your hip: {npc} and three neighbours are telling the story of the fox on the hill road, the one that walks beside students. It has three tails, says one. It ate a magistrate, says another. {npc}, who loves a story, says it is beautiful and lonely and only wants to be a person. They all turn to you. "What do you think?"
events.arc: A Year in a Borrowed Face

choices.text: "I think it is probably very ugly and smells of wet dog."

effects.log: The well laughs. {npc} pouts and defends the fox's honour all the way home. You have learned the best place for a fox to hide: inside a joke about itself.

choices.text: "I think {npc} is right."

mem.note: agreed with me about the fox of the hill road

effects.log: {npc} is delighted to have an ally, and tells you the story again on the way home, in full, with improvements. In the story the fox is much braver than you are. You do not correct it.

choices.text: "I think foxes should be left alone."

effects.log: An awkward silence, then somebody changes the subject to the price of salt. But {npc} glances at you sideways, all the way home, the way people look at someone who said a little more than they meant.

events.text: A neighbour has died, an old carpenter, and the bier is going out to the hill at dawn. The village needs a lead singer for the bier-song, the one who walks in front ringing the bell and calling the verses, and the old singer has a cough. {npc}, the carpenter's eldest, asks you, because you have a good voice and no family here to mourn.
events.arc: A Year in a Borrowed Face

choices.text: Sing it. Ring the bell, call the verses, all the way to the grave

mem.note: sang my father to the hill

ok.log: You know where the dead go on this hill better than anyone in the village. The verses come out like water. The bier-bearers keep step, and weep, and the carpenter goes into the earth sung properly. Afterwards {npc} holds your hands and cannot speak.

fail.log: Your voice is fine; your eyes are the trouble. Walking up toward the old graves at dawn, with the cold breath coming off them, your eyes go gold, and a bearer stumbles. You finish the song looking at the ground.

choices.text: Say you do not know the verses, and walk with the mourners instead

effects.log: You walk at the back. The old singer coughs through it, and it is enough. At the grave you stand very still, a few paces from a fox's earth you know well.

events.text: Midnight, and a traveller, {npc}, knocks at your door: lost, frightened, a lantern burning low. The road to the next town goes through the old graveyard on the hill, and something in the graveyard has been leading {him} round in circles for two hours with lights. You know what it is. It is a very young fox of the hill, playing.
events.arc: A Year in a Borrowed Face

choices.text: Walk {him} through the graveyard yourself, with your own lantern

effects.log: Through the mounds, past the little lights, which go out one by one as you pass, embarrassed. {npc} gets to the town by dawn and tells everyone about the kind stranger who was not afraid of the graveyard. The young fox gets a talking-to the next night.

choices.text: Give {him} a bed, and go and have words with the young fox

effects.log: {npc} sleeps on your floor. On the hill, a very young fox with one tail gets the lecture of its life from something with several, and swears never to lead a traveller astray again, unless they deserve it.

choices.text: Give {him} directions the long way round, and shut the door

effects.log: The long way is longer. {npc} gets there at noon, tired and cross, and never comes back through your town. The young fox goes on playing in the graveyard. Someone else will deal with it.

events.text: Chuseok, and the full moon, and the whole village out on the threshing floor: the circle dance going round and round, wrestling for an ox, rice cakes in pine needles. {npc} grabs your hand and pulls you into the circle. Full moon. In company. Under that much light, the tails are very close to the surface.
events.arc: A Year in a Borrowed Face

choices.text: Dance. All night. Hold the face with both hands

ok.log: Round and round under the moon, singing the old circle song with the whole village. The moon goes into the bead and into the face both. You are a person all night, more than you have ever been. At dawn you go home and sleep a whole day as a fox.

fail.log: At the top of the night, the moon right overhead, a child points at your shadow on the threshing floor and says, "Look, it has a tail." Everyone looks. It does not, by then. But everyone looked.

choices.text: Pull free, laughing, and say you are dizzy

effects.log: {npc} lets you go, disappointed. You sit at the edge in the shadow of the straw stacks and watch the circle go round under the moon, and that is a kind of being there too.

choices.text: Dance one round, then slip out of the circle into the dark

effects.log: One round. The moon on everyone's faces, yours included, the singing, the hands. Then you let go and step back into the dark, and the circle closes behind you without a gap, as if you had never been in it.

events.text: The household register is being redone: every three years the clerks come round with brushes and books, and every house must give its people, their ages, their fathers' names. {npc}, the clerk, is at your door with the book open. You have been in this village far longer than the face should allow, and the last register says you were thirty then. The clerk is doing the sum.
events.arc: A Year in a Borrowed Face

choices.text: Give an age that fits the face, not the register, and smile

ok.log: {npc} looks at the old entry, at you, at the old entry. "A clerk's mistake, last time," {npc} decides, and corrects it, and you are a believable age again, officially. Clerks prefer a mistake to a mystery.

fail.log: {npc} looks at the old entry, at you, and does not correct it. {npc} writes your age as it should be, far too old, and looks up at a face of thirty, and says nothing at all, and goes to the next house very fast.

choices.text: Give the true sum, and say your family ages well

effects.log: "Very well," says {npc}, writing it down. "Remarkably well." By the next market the whole village knows your secret is ginseng. Thirty people ask you where you dig it.

choices.text: Be away from home every day the clerk comes, all month

effects.log: You are at the market, the hill, the next village. {npc} comes four times and gives up and copies the old entry. You will have to do something about this before the next register.

events.text: {npc}, a neighbour's child of about nine, has found out that you can do the shadow-animals on the wall better than anyone: the rabbit, the crane, the dog. Tonight, by the lamp, {npc} asks for a fox. "A fox with lots of tails," {npc} says. "Like in the story."
events.arc: A Year in a Borrowed Face

choices.text: Make it with your hands. Only your hands

effects.log: A fox, with two fingers for ears and the rest of your hand for a tail. One tail. {npc} demands more. You do your best with two hands. It is a very good fox. It is not as good as the one you could make.

choices.text: Let one real tail into the shadow, just one, among the hand-tails

mem.note: saw the best shadow fox in the world

effects.log: The shadow on the wall has many tails, and one of them moves on its own. {npc} screams with delight, not fear. Children do not know enough to be afraid of the right things. {npc} tells everyone, and nobody believes {him}, and {he} never forgets it.

choices.text: Say the lamp oil is low, and send {npc} home

effects.log: You blow the lamp out. {npc} goes home sulking. The dark room is safer, and very quiet.

events.text: Spring, and a matchmaker has not come, but a neighbour has: {npc}, who wants to borrow the ox you do not have and, failing that, wants to talk, and talk, about the neighbour on the other side, who is certainly a thief, and the neighbour beyond, who is certainly worse, and you, who are, {npc} says warmly, the only decent person on this street. You know {npc} says that to everyone.
events.arc: A Year in a Borrowed Face

choices.text: Listen kindly, and say nothing about anybody

effects.log: A whole afternoon. {npc} leaves happy, having said everything, and you know every quarrel on the street. That is useful. A fox knows the paths through a field; a person in a borrowed face knows the paths through a street.

choices.text: Say something unkind about the thief next door, to fit in

effects.log: {npc} is thrilled, and repeats it everywhere, with your name on it. The street decides you are one of them. You did not like what you said. You notice, with interest, that it worked.

events.text: Your face has been on this street for years. {npc}, who sells bean curd at the corner and has watched everyone come and go for forty, stops you with a hand on your sleeve and says, quietly, with great kindness: "You have not changed at all. Not a line. People are starting to talk. You should go away for a while, I think. Come back as someone's cousin."
events.arc: A Year in a Borrowed Face

choices.text: Thank {npc}, and take the advice

effects.log: A sick relative in the south. You are gone by the market day. The street wonders for a season and then forgets. {npc} never forgets, and sends a block of bean curd to the empty house every new year, which the neighbours think is very strange.

choices.text: Ask {npc} why tell you, and not the street

mem.note: warned the one who never ages

effects.log: "Because you have been kind to my grandchildren," {npc} says, "and I do not care what you are." You stand very still. It is the first time anyone has said that to you, in any face.

choices.text: Laugh it off. Good skin runs in the family

effects.log: {npc} looks at you sadly and lets go of your sleeve. "As you like," {npc} says. The street goes on talking.
